script.say:
It is the fifth of June, 2015. In New Delhi, the global chief executive of Nestlé stands in front of the press. He says the noodles are safe. The same day, India's food regulator orders every variant of Maggi to be withdrawn and recalled.
Across the country, about three and a half million shops sell this packet. Some are supermarkets. Most are small shops, with a few packets hanging in a net by the counter.
Within days, all of it has to come back. Every carton in every warehouse. Every loose packet on every shelf. The chain that carried this packet out for thirty years now has to carry it back.
On the back of each packet there is one small line of print. A batch code. A date of manufacture. A best-before date. On the worst day in this brand's history, that line of print matters more than the advertising, the reach and the thirty years of goodwill.
script.sees: VO: VO. Kirana shelves with yellow packets in nets, slow push in. Then archive of a New Delhi press conference, June 2015. Then a hand turning a packet over to the printed batch code.
script.title: Cold open: the fifth of June

script.say:
I want to ask one question in this episode. What is a system for, when the worst day comes?
Not on a normal Monday. On the day someone outside your business asks a hard question, and wants the answer today. And whether your records can give that answer, or only your memory.
This is Built to Run. Stories of businesses that run on systems, not on memory.
script.sees: FULL: FULL. Palak at her desk, to camera.
script.title: The question

script.say:
Let me start with the good years, because this is not a story about a weak company.
Nestlé launched Maggi noodles in India in 1983. At the time there was no quick hot snack a mother could make between school and dinner. A samosa or a kachori could not be made in a few minutes. Maggi offered a hot snack in two minutes.
One of the people on the launch team has described how they thought about it. Children were the audience. The mother was the person who decided. Few homes watched much television then, so they sold through displays in shops and through promotions at schools and in parks.
It worked slowly, and then completely. Two minutes became part of how the country spoke. Hostel rooms. Hill-station stalls. Late nights in offices. For many children, the first thing they learned to cook. A packet that cost a few rupees became a habit in millions of homes.
You will hear many large numbers about this brand in feature stories. A lot of them cannot be traced to any source. In this episode I will give you only the ones that can.
script.sees: FULL: FULL. Palak to camera.
script.title: Act 1: Thirty years of reach

script.say:
Behind the promise was a distribution system that very few companies in India could match.
By 2015, Maggi was made in five factories. It moved through thirty-eight distribution centres that Nestlé ran directly. From there it went to about fourteen hundred distributors. And from them, by Nestlé's own estimate, to about three and a half million shops.
That is the reach that put a yellow packet in a hill-station stall, a college hostel and a kirana shop in a small town in Madhya Pradesh.
How much of the market did it hold? The answer depends on who measured. Euromonitor put it at sixty-three percent of the noodle market in 2014. Nestlé India later said its share before the crisis was about seventy-five percent. Nielsen data, as reported in the press, said seventy-seven percent in January 2015. One brokerage said about eighty. Whichever number you take, this was the brand that defined the category.
script.sees: PIP: PIP. GFX-2, the chain diagram builds left to right: five factories, 38 distribution centres, about 1,400 distributors, about 3.5 million shops.
script.title: The machine behind the packet

script.say:
Now, you may be thinking, I run a forty-person firm in Indore. I am not Nestlé.
That is true. Nestlé India is a listed company. It had more than seven thousand employees. It has a global parent with its own laboratories and lawyers. You will never face a national regulator and a High Court in the same summer.
But think about the shape of the problem.
You make something, or you deliver something. It goes out through people you do not fully see. A dealer. A sub-dealer. A site supervisor. A junior in your office who sends the file to the client.
One day a customer calls and says, something is wrong with what you sent. Which lot was it? Who else got material from the same lot? What did your quality check show that day? Who signed it off?
In many firms, the answer to each of those questions is a person. The owner remembers. The dispatch man remembers. The accountant can find it, if you give him two days.
And the owner, meanwhile, is on the phone. To the dispatch man. To the dealer. To the supervisor. The same question, in different words, all afternoon. Every owner knows the call that ends with one tired question: "Ho gaya?"
I have sat at that desk. In my family's firm, before we designed our system, the answer to most questions was a person. Usually the same person.
script.sees: FULL: FULL. Palak to camera.
script.title: Your desk in this story

script.say:
That is what I mean when I say work needs a home. A name. A date. A next step. A place anyone can look, without asking.
Maggi had that home for every packet that left the factory. What the year 2015 tested was everything that came after the factory. And whether the records could answer a question that came from outside, in the form the outsider wanted.
Let us look at the system piece by piece.
script.sees: PIP: PIP. Desk shot, a diary and sticky notes, then a phone ringing.
script.title: The work that has no home

script.say:
Every story in this series is read through the same six questions.
Where does the work live? How can anyone see the state of it? Who finds out when something slips, and how fast? How are mistakes caught before they reach the customer? What happens when the person at the top is not there? And what happened when it broke?
For Maggi, the sixth question is the reason we are here. So let us take the first five, one at a time, and look at the piece of the system that answers each.
script.sees: FULL: FULL. Palak to camera. Then PIP with GFX-9, the six questions card.
script.title: Act 2: Five pieces of one system

script.say:
The first mechanism is the smallest. It is the batch code.
Every packet of Maggi carries a batch number, a date of manufacture and a best-before date. In a food business, that line of print is the home of the work. It tells you which plant made it, on which day, in which run.
Here is how well it worked in this story. In April 2015, the food authorities in Lucknow asked Nestlé to recall one batch. Nestlé could say exactly what that batch was. It was made in February 2014. It was about two lakh packs. And its best-before date had already passed, in November 2014.
That is a good record. One batch, named, dated and sized, on demand.
Think about what a batch record in any food plant has to connect. The flour, the oil, the spice mix, each with its own supplier lot. The line it ran on. The shift. The checks done before release. When a question comes about one packet, a good batch record lets you walk backwards to every input, and forwards to every carton.
That is all traceability means. It is not a software word. It is the ability to walk the chain in both directions.
So the first question of this series, where does the work live, has a clear answer at the factory gate. It lives on the pack and in the batch record. Not in someone's memory.
script.sees: PIP: PIP. Close-up of a batch code under a desk lamp. GFX-10 labels each part: plant, batch, date made, best before.
script.title: Mechanism one: the line of print on the pack

script.say:
The second mechanism is the distribution chain.
From factory to distribution centre, Nestlé could see everything. From distribution centre to distributor, it had an invoice for every carton.
But look at the last step. Nestlé estimated that about half of the three and a half million shops that sold Maggi were not served directly by its own distributor network. They bought through wholesalers and smaller traders. The company could not see them.
This is the second question of the series. How can anyone see the state of the work? Up to the distributor, the state was visible. Beyond that, for about half the shops, it was not.
Nothing about that was careless. That is how most goods reach most Indian shops. The chain was designed to push packets out, as widely and as cheaply as possible. It was never designed to pull them back.
This is not only a food problem. A pipe maker sells through dealers. A pharma distributor sells through chemists. A garment unit sells through agents in five states. In each case, the company knows its first customer well and its last customer barely at all.
I want you to remember that sentence. A chain designed to push cannot pull.
script.sees: PIP: PIP. GFX-2 again. The last box, 3.5 million shops, splits in two: half shaded navy, half left pale.
script.title: Mechanism two: the chain that pushes

script.say:
The third mechanism is the test record. This is how a food company catches an error before it reaches the customer.
Nestlé said it tested about a thousand batches in its own accredited laboratory. It sent samples from about six hundred batches to an outside laboratory. Together, it said, they covered about a hundred and twenty-five million packets. And all were within the limits.
That is a large body of evidence. Most companies of any size would be glad to have it.
So the fourth question, how are errors caught, has an answer too. There was a check. There were records of the check.
But here is the turn in the story. The regulator was not asking about Nestlé's tests. It was asking about its own.
script.sees: PIP: PIP. Laboratory footage, a technician with sample tubes. GFX: two numbers appear, "about 1,000 batches in Nestlé's lab" and "about 600 batches at an outside lab".
script.title: Mechanism three: the test record

script.say:
There is one more record in this story that is easy to miss. The words printed on the pack.
The pack said no added MSG. The company said that was true, because it did not add MSG. The regulator read it differently, because the tests showed glutamate, which Nestlé said came naturally from the ingredients.
Whatever the chemistry, here is the systems point. Every claim you make to a customer is a record too. A promise on a quotation. A delivery date on an order. A line on a test certificate. If you cannot defend it with evidence, in the customer's terms, it turns against you on the worst day.
After the crisis, Nestlé took that line off the pack.
script.sees: PIP: PIP. BR-01, the back of a pack, slow pan across the printed text. Then GFX: "Every claim is a record."
script.title: A line on the pack is a promise

script.say:
The regulator's findings were about specific samples, tested in specific labs. Its order said three things. That lead was above the permitted limit of two and a half parts per million. That the line on the pack, no added MSG, was misleading. And that one variant, the oats masala noodles, had been sold without the required approval.
Nestlé disagreed on the science. It said the regulator had tested the parts of the product separately, rather than the noodles as they are eaten. It said it did not add MSG, and that glutamate occurs naturally in ingredients like groundnut protein, onion and wheat flour.
I am not going to tell you who was right on the chemistry. A court and several laboratories did that work, and we will come to them.
What I want you to see is the shape of the gap. The company had many records. They answered the company's own question, in its own method, in labs it chose. The outside question was different. It was about a sample the company did not pick, tested a way the company did not choose, and about one sentence printed on its own pack.
The records that would settle that question, on the same day, in a form the outsider would accept, did not exist.
The man who took over Nestlé India that summer, Suresh Narayanan, later described the ban as the result of a major breakdown in communication with the government. That is his reading, and I think it is an honest one.
script.sees: PIP: PIP. GFX-5: a question arrives from the left, labelled "the regulator's question", and meets a record on the right, labelled "the company's record". They do not quite line up.
script.title: The question from outside

script.say:
The fourth mechanism is the feedback loop. Who finds out when something slips, and how fast?
Let me walk you through the dates, because they tell the whole story.
March 2014. Food safety officers in Barabanki, in Uttar Pradesh, pick up Maggi samples in a routine check.
April 2014. The state laboratory in Gorakhpur reports a problem with the no added MSG line on the label. Nestlé appeals.
The sample is sent for a second test to the Central Food Laboratory in Kolkata. That report is dated the seventh of April, 2015. It says the sample has seventeen point two parts per million of lead, against a limit of two and a half.
Thirtieth of April, 2015. The authorities in Lucknow ask Nestlé to recall that batch.
May. The news breaks. Within days it is everywhere.
So, from the sample to the recall order, the loop took about thirteen months. It ran through a sample bag, a laboratory, an appeal and the post. And by the time the answer came back, the batch had passed its best-before date months earlier.
Nestlé argued that the Kolkata result was high because the sample had been left open for a long time before it was tested. The regulator disputed that. Again, I am not the judge of it. But notice what both sides were arguing about. Not the noodles in the shops. The handling of one sample, over thirteen months. The record of what happened to the sample became as important as the sample itself.
Then the public loop started. That one ran in days.
The third question of the series is about exactly this. A slow loop inside, and a fast loop outside, is the most dangerous combination a business can have. You find out last.
script.sees: PIP: PIP. GFX-1, a timeline drawn left to right. March 2014. April 2014. April 2015. 30 April 2015. May 2015. 5 June 2015. The gap between the first and fourth points is shaded and labelled "thirteen months".
script.title: Mechanism four: the feedback loop

script.say:
The fifth question is the one I ask every owner. What happens when you are not there?
For a company this size, the question becomes: does the system depend on one senior person, or does it run as a process?
Two things in this story suggest the second.
First, the recall itself. Nestlé announced the withdrawal on the fifth of June. By its own account, the recall was fully running two days later. About fifty people in the supply chain team worked on it full time. And the rest of the company kept supplying its other brands as normal.
Think about who actually ran that recall. Not the people in the news. Distributors who took back stock. Shopkeepers who handed over packets and waited for their credit. Truck drivers. Kiln operators. None of them could phone the head of the company for every decision. They needed a process, and they had one.
Second, the way quality is wired. Nestlé has described a structure in which the technical director reports to the head of Nestlé India on a dotted line, and has a straight line to the head office in Switzerland. The point is simple. No country head, however senior, can trade quality for a sales target.
And the top person did change. A new head of Nestlé India took over in the middle of the crisis. The recall did not stop for that.
So the fifth question has a mixed answer. The recall did not depend on one person. But the relationship with the regulator, by the company's own later account, had not been built into the system at all.
script.sees: PIP: PIP. Warehouse footage, cartons and a forklift. GFX: "operational in two days" and "about 50 people, full time".
script.title: Mechanism five: when the top person is not in the room

script.say:
Let me put the five pieces side by side.
The work had a home on every pack. Strong.
The chain could see up to the distributor. Beyond that, for about half the shops, it could not. Weak at the edge.
The test records were large. But they answered the company's question, not the regulator's. A gap.
The feedback loop from the shop shelf back to the company took thirteen months. Slow.
The recall ran as a process, not on one person. Strong.
None of this is unusual. Most good businesses look like this. Strong at the centre. Weaker at the edges. And slow to hear from the edges. If you drew the same five boxes for your own business tonight, I suspect many of you would shade the same two.
Now watch what happens when all five are tested at once.
script.sees: PIP: PIP. K1, Palak's hand sketches five boxes in a row: pack code, chain, test record, feedback loop, process. She shades two of them amber.
script.title: What the system looked like on the eve of the crisis

script.say:
Now the sixth question. What happened when it broke?
The test began on the fifth of June, 2015.
Delhi had already reported that ten of thirteen samples of the seasoning mix were above the lead limit, and banned sales for fifteen days. Gujarat reported twenty-seven of thirty-nine samples and banned sales for thirty days. Other states followed.
That day, Nestlé said it would take Maggi off the shelves. In its own words, it did so "despite the product being safe". The same day, the national food regulator ordered all nine variants withdrawn and recalled.
script.sees: FULL: FULL. Palak to camera.
script.title: Act 3: The test

script.say:
Nestlé's first estimate was twenty-seven thousand, four hundred and twenty tonnes.
About forty percent of that was no longer in cartons. It was loose packets, on shop shelves and in people's homes. To bring them back, Nestlé had to buy about one point four million cartons from across the country.
To carry all of it in one load would take about two thousand five hundred trucks. But nothing moves in one load. Stock moves from shop to distributor, from distributor to depot, from depot to the point of destruction. Many thousands of truck journeys.
At every step, money changes hands in reverse. Credit notes. Refunds. Cash. Each one has to be recorded, or someone is short at the end of the month.
The noodles were burnt as fuel in five cement kilns. Together, those kilns could take about seven hundred tonnes a day. That alone meant at least forty days of burning.
script.sees: PIP: PIP. GFX-3, a number that counts up to 27,420 tonnes. Then trucks on a highway, then hands packing loose packets into a carton.
script.title: Pulling a country's worth of noodles back

script.say:
Here is the figure I find most telling.
The first estimate was about twenty-seven thousand tonnes. By the first of September, by Nestlé's own account to the Supreme Court, about thirty-eight thousand tonnes had been destroyed. And in 2016 the Court allowed Nestlé to destroy a further five hundred and fifty tonnes of expired stock.
I do not read that gap as a failure of honesty. The sources do not say why the figure grew, and some of it may be stock held in the company's own depots. But the point stands. With a chain this wide, you find out how much is out there only when it comes back.
That is the second lesson of this episode in one number. You cannot recall what you cannot trace.
script.sees: PIP: PIP. GFX-3 continues, the counter moves from 27,420 to about 38,000 tonnes. Then a cement plant at dusk.
script.title: The number that grew

script.say:
Nestlé India valued the stock in the market at about two hundred and ten crore rupees. The stock and materials in its own factories and depots, at about a hundred and ten crore more. That was before the cost of collecting, carrying and burning it.
For the quarter from April to June 2015, Nestlé India reported a net loss of about sixty-four crore rupees. A year earlier, in the same quarter, it had made a profit of about two hundred and eighty-eight crore. Most reports said it was the company's first quarterly loss in at least fifteen years.
And the share. For five months, a brand that had held most of its market sold nothing at all.
script.sees: PIP: PIP. GFX-7, three cards: "Rs 210 crore of stock in the market", "Rs 110 crore in factories and depots", "Rs 64.4 crore net loss, April to June 2015".
script.title: The cost

script.say:
On the thirteenth of August, 2015, the Bombay High Court set aside the national ban.
I want to be exact about what it found, because this part is often told wrongly.
The court held that the order had been passed without a fair hearing, and that the samples had been tested in laboratories that were not accredited by the national accreditation board. It did not declare the noodles safe. It ordered new tests. Five samples of every variant, at three accredited laboratories, in Punjab, Hyderabad and Jaipur, within six weeks. No manufacture and no sale until then.
All ninety samples cleared. New batches from three factories were tested and cleared. On the ninth of November, 2015, Maggi came back, first in about a hundred towns. An online sale of sixty thousand packs sold out in about five minutes. By the thirtieth of November, all five factories were running again.
From ban to shelf. Five months.
script.sees: PIP: PIP. Exterior of the Bombay High Court. Then a court file tied with tape.
script.title: What the court found

script.say:
The way back came in steps. Press reports of Nielsen data put Maggi at forty-two percent in January 2016. Nestlé itself put it at about fifty-seven in June. Its annual report for 2016 said about sixty. By 2018, the company said a little over sixty. India is now the largest market for Maggi in the world.
And the company changed things. It took the no added MSG line off the pack. It said it would run a round-the-clock consumer helpline. It said it would work with rival companies to help build the government's testing capacity, with laboratories and training. It said it would rebuild its ties with the owners of almost four million shops.
The rebuild was not a return to the old system. It was a chance to build a better one.
script.sees: PIP: PIP. GFX-4, a share line: about 75 before, nothing for five months, 42 in January 2016, about 57 in June 2016, about 60 at the end of 2016, a little over 60 in 2018.
script.title: The rebuild

script.say:
Let me bring this back to your business. Four lessons. Each one comes from a moment in the story.
The first lesson. A batch record is a home for work.
When the authorities in Lucknow asked about one batch, Nestlé could say when it was made, how many packs it held, and when it expired. That is the record doing its job.
In your business, what is the batch? If you make parts, it is the lot. If you trade, it is the consignment. If you run a CA practice or a consultancy, it is the client file and the version of the working you sent.
Each one needs a home. A number. A date. A name against it. And the next step. If the only record of which customer got which lot is in the dispatch man's head, the work does not have a home. It has a tenant.
One more thing. The record has to be made at the moment the work happens. Not at the end of the week, from memory. A batch record written up on Saturday is a story, not a record.
script.sees: FULL: FULL. Palak to camera.
script.title: Act 4: What this means for a business of 15 to 100 people

script.say:
The second lesson. You cannot recall what you cannot trace.
Nestlé could see every carton up to its distributors. Beyond that, for about half the shops, it could not. And the amount it destroyed ended about ten thousand tonnes above its first estimate.
Ask yourself one plain question this week. If a supplier told you that one lot of raw material was faulty, could you list every order it went into, and every customer who received those orders, by this evening?
For many owners the honest answer is, I would have to ask three people and wait two days. That is not a discipline problem. It is a design problem. The sheet that records the lot at the gate also has to record where it went at dispatch. One column. Filled in every time.
script.sees: FULL: FULL, cutting to PIP over a dispatch bay in an Indore-area unit, cartons with a lot number written on the side.
script.title: Lesson two: you cannot recall what you cannot trace

script.say:
The third lesson. The system has to be able to answer a question from outside on the same day.
Nestlé had large numbers of test records. But the outside question came in a different shape. Different samples, different labs, one line on the pack. It took a court and five months to settle.
Your outside questions are smaller, but they come. A large customer runs a supplier audit. A bank asks for stock statements and debtor ageing before renewal. A GST notice asks about one invoice from two years ago. A client asks who approved a figure in last year's return.
The question is never, do you have the information somewhere. The question is, can you produce it today, in the form they asked for, without the owner sitting up till midnight.
Here is a test you can run this Friday. Pick one order from last month, at random. Ask your team where every part of it came from, and where every part of it went. If it is minutes, you have a system. If it is days, you have people who are good at remembering.
In my family's firm, when a lender asks a question, the answer comes from the sheet. Not from someone remembering. That is the only reason we can answer it the same day.
script.sees: FULL: FULL.
script.title: Lesson three: answer the outside question the same day

script.say:
The fourth lesson has two halves.
A crisis is answered by records, not by memory. In June 2015, a brand with thirty years of goodwill could not stay on the shelf on the strength of that goodwill. The shelf came back only when ninety samples, tested in labs the court chose, came back clear. Goodwill buys you patience. Records buy you the answer.
And the rebuild is a chance to make the system better than it was. Nestlé took a line off its pack that it could not defend in the regulator's terms. It said it would put a helpline in place. It offered to help build testing capacity outside its own walls.
In a smaller firm, the bad month is the moment the team will accept a change they would have resisted in a good one. A lost customer. A wrong dispatch. A missed filing date. That is the week to give the work a home, not the week to find someone to blame.
People at Nestlé have said they learned more in those five months than in the years before. The question is whether the learning is written into the system, or only into the memory of the people who lived through it. Memory leaves when they do.
[your own line]
script.sees: FULL: FULL.
script.title: Lesson four: records, not memory, and a better rebuild

script.say:
Maggi took two minutes to cook and five months to come back. The two minutes were the product. The five months were the system being tested.
So here are the six answers, in one breath. The work lived on the pack and in the batch record. Its state was visible up to the distributor, and not beyond. The feedback loop inside took thirteen months. Errors were checked by a large body of tests, but in the company's own terms. The recall did not depend on one person. And when it broke, the brand came back in five months, and came back changed.
None of that needed a hero. It needed records that existed before the bad day, and people who knew where to find them.
This is the work I do now. In my family's firm, VSP Consultants, I designed one place where every piece of work lives, with a name, a date and a next step, so that the answer to a hard question is on the sheet and not in someone's head. Now I set up the same kind of system for owners of businesses with fifteen to a hundred people, one process at a time.
Start with one question. If something went wrong with one order today, could you trace it by the evening?
If you want to see how this looks for your business, book a 30-minute call. The link is in the description.
script.sees: FULL: FULL. Palak at her desk. Slow push in.
script.title: Close

script.say: Thank you for watching. Next week, another business, another system.
script.sees: FULL: FULL to end card. Navy field, ivory type: "Built to Run. Stories of businesses that run on systems, not on memory." Below it the booking link and the Venture Drafters wordmark.
script.title: End card

snapshot.notes:
Built to Run: Stories, episode 03: Maggi. The two minutes that took five months.. Source: Marketing/case-studies/03-maggi.md (script, b-roll list, slide outline, fact sheet, sources, cut-downs). Fortnightly Monday slot 2026-12-07, 11:00.

Do not claim (from the fact sheet):
- That Maggi held 90 percent of the market for 25 years. It appears in features, not in audited data.
- That Maggi's share was exactly 80 percent. Use "about three quarters, by Nestlé's own account", or give the range.
- That the Bombay High Court declared Maggi safe. It ruled on procedure and accredited labs and ordered fresh tests.
- That Nestlé was fined Rs 640 crore. That was the government's claim before the NCDRC, and it was dismissed in April 2024.
- That the lead was "17 times" the limit. It was 17.2 ppm against 2.5 ppm, about seven times.
- That Maggi "contained MSG" as a finding of added MSG. The charge was about the *No added MSG* label; Nestlé says the glutamate was natural.
- That Nestlé now tests every batch at NABL labs, or runs "250-plus extra tests". We found no company source for either.
- That Nestlé paid Ambuja Cements Rs 20 crore to burn the noodles. The company did not confirm it.
- That the recall cost Rs 420 crore, or Rs 500 crore. The traceable company figures are Rs 210 crore plus Rs 110 crore of stock, and the Rs 451.66 crore exceptional item.
- That this was Nestlé India's "first loss ever". Reports range from fifteen years to three decades; say "first quarterly loss in at least fifteen years, by most accounts".
- That Maggi's share "fell to zero" as a measured figure. The product was off the shelf; no share was measured.
- That the rise from 27,420 to about 38,000 tonnes was caused by shops outside Nestlé's view. No source gives the cause, and the larger figure may include stock held in Nestlé's own depots.
- That Delhi's 10 failing samples were noodles. They were samples of the seasoning mix.
- That Edelweiss estimated Maggi's pre-ban share. We found no such estimate.
- That the 550 tonnes was destroyed on a stated date. We have the Court's permission (October 2016), not a report of the destruction.
- That Nestlé "set up" a helpline or joint testing laboratories. We have only its stated plans.
- The reported comparison of Rs 445 crore advertising spend against Rs 19 crore quality testing spend. It comes from one accounting line and may not capture all quality costs.
- --

2. We could not verify any figure for "tests per batch" or testing frequency after the relaunch. 3. Sensitivity: the story involves a regulator, a High Court record and a government consumer case that Nestlé won in April 2024. We found no appeal, but this should be checked against NCDRC or Supreme Court records before publication. script.say:
It is a little after six in the morning, in a village in Anand district, in Gujarat. A woman walks to a small room at the end of the lane. She carries a steel can. There are four people ahead of her. Nobody pushes.
At the window, the secretary pours her milk into a measure. The weight shows on a small screen. A little milk goes into a machine. Within a minute, a slip prints. It shows the date, the shift, her member number, the litres, the fat, the rate and the amount.
She reads it. She folds it. She goes home.
Nobody argued. Nobody phoned anyone. Nobody senior was in the room. This evening she will come back and do it again. So will about 36 lakh other farmers, in about 18,600 villages across Gujarat.
This scene is a composite. I have put it together from the dairy board's own handbook for collection staff. But some version of it happens twice a day, every day.
script.sees: VO: VO. Dawn in a Gujarat village. A woman walks down a lane with a steel can. A small room with a counter window, a short queue. Milk poured, a sample drawn, a slip printing, the slip folded into a pocket. Lower-third caption: "A composite scene, drawn from NDDB's procurement handbook."
script.title: Six in the morning, a village in Anand district

script.say:
I wanted to understand that room. Because it does something most of our businesses cannot do. It settles a payment, fairly, with lakhs of people, every day, without the owner standing there.
So the question for this episode is simple. How does a business owned by lakhs of small farmers pay every one of them correctly, on a day they know, without anyone having to remember, argue or chase?
This is Built to Run. Stories of businesses that run on systems, not on memory.
script.sees: FULL: FULL. Palak at her desk, a steel milk can and a folded slip beside her laptop.
script.title: The question

script.say:
Let me start with a desk I know.
A supplier calls at ten. He wants to know when his payment will come. You are not sure. Accounts knows, or thinks it knows. You call accounts. Accounts calls you back at twelve.
At two, a worker says the rate on his slip is wrong. He may be right. He may not be. Either way, it comes to you, because you are the only person both sides will believe.
At five, a customer says the last lot was short. Was it checked before it left? Somebody says yes. Nobody can show it.
None of this is a big problem. Each one takes five minutes. But each one needs you. By the evening, you have been the accounts desk, the quality check and the referee. Everything has come through you.
I saw this in my family's firm, VSP Consultants, before we changed how the work was held. The owner is not slow. The owner is simply the only place where the answer lives.
Now let me take you somewhere the same three questions come up lakhs of times a day. And almost none of them reach the top.
script.sees: FULL: FULL. Palak to camera. Cutaways to the desk: sticky notes, a diary, a phone face down.
script.title: Your desk, this morning

script.say:
Go back to Kaira district, in central Gujarat, in the 1940s.
The farmers here kept buffaloes. Their milk went to Bombay under a government milk scheme. The scheme bought from a private dairy at Anand called Polson, which held the right to collect milk across the district. Between Polson and the villages stood the milk contractors.
The union's own history puts it plainly. Nobody had fixed the price paid to the farmer. The contractor fixed it. The farmer sold at that price, or did not sell at all.
That is the position of every small supplier with one buyer. The price is a favour. So is the payment day.
The farmers went to Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel. He gave them specific advice. Form your own cooperative. Own your own processing. Ask the government to buy from you. If it refuses, stop selling to the middlemen, and accept the loss for a while.
On the fourth of January 1946, at a meeting in Samarkha village, the farmers resolved to do exactly that. The government refused. So the farmers stopped selling milk, for fifteen days. Bombay's milk scheme nearly collapsed. The Milk Commissioner came to Anand and accepted their demand.
On the fourteenth of December 1946, the Kaira District Cooperative Milk Producers' Union was registered. Its chairman was Tribhuvandas Patel, a Gandhian and a freedom fighter from Anand.
script.sees: PIP: PIP. Archive photographs of Anand and Kaira district in the 1940s. GFX-01, the map of Gujarat with Kheda and Anand marked. Portraits of Sardar Patel and Tribhuvandas Patel as they are named.
script.title: Kaira, 1946: a price set by someone else

script.say:
The strike won the farmers a buyer. It did not yet solve the harder problem.
Think about the transaction itself. A farmer with two buffaloes brings a few litres. Someone has to measure it, judge its quality, write it down, and pay for it, on some day.
At every one of those steps, a person with more power can cheat a person with less. A thumb on the scale. A low reading. A missing entry. A payment that comes late, or not at all. Under the contractors, each step depended on trusting one man.
Tribhuvandas Patel insisted on two rules from the start. Every village society was open to every milk producer, regardless of caste, creed or community. And every member had one vote, whatever his wealth. The union's own account records both.
Those rules settled who belonged. The next question was harder. How could a small room in each village treat everyone the same, twice a day, with nobody from Anand watching?
In May 1949, a young engineer arrived in Anand to serve out a government bond at the creamery. His name was Verghese Kurien. In his autobiography, I Too Had a Dream, he called the town "excruciatingly unexciting and conservative." He meant to leave as soon as he could. Tribhuvandas Patel asked him to stay a little and help set up the union's equipment.
He stayed for the rest of his working life. But notice the order. The farmers built the union first.
script.sees: PIP: PIP. GFX-03: one farmer, one contractor, four questions between them: weight, quality, record, payment day. Then a portrait of Verghese Kurien and the cover of his autobiography.
script.title: The real problem was trust

script.say:
Here is what I noticed when I read the handbook that India's National Dairy Development Board gives to milk procurement staff. It describes the village counter in plain steps. There is no slogan in it.
There are five mechanisms. A fixed rhythm. A test done in front of the person. A record the farmer carries home. A payment on a known day. And one rule, the same in every village.
Let me take them one at a time.
script.sees: FULL: FULL. Palak to camera, the NDDB handbook open on the desk beside her.
script.title: Five things the counter does

script.say:
The first mechanism is the rhythm.
Every morning and every evening, members bring their milk to the society at set times. The handbook lists collection twice a day as the society's first function. The truck from the union arrives on the society's fixed schedule, picks up the milk, and leaves. If you are late, the milk misses the truck.
This rhythm was not a management idea. Milk forced it. Milk spoils. Buffaloes are milked morning and evening. So the business had to move twice a day, every day, through festivals, and through the days when the secretary has a fever.
But look at what the rhythm does for management. Nobody needs to be reminded to bring milk. Nobody needs to ask the driver when he is coming. Nobody needs to ask whether collection is open today. The time itself is the instruction.
In June 1948, the union was pasteurising about 250 litres a day from two village societies. By the end of that year, 432 farmers had joined, and the union handled 5,000 litres a day. That growth did not need more supervision. It needed more people arriving at the same two times.
In most of our firms, the rhythm is the owner. Dispatch happens when he asks. The review happens when he remembers. Payment happens when someone chases. Take the owner away, and the rhythm stops.
At the village counter, the rhythm belongs to the day, not to a person.
script.sees: PIP: PIP. Morning queue at a collection centre, then the same counter in evening light. Cans lifted onto a truck. GFX-04: a clock with two marks, morning and evening, and a truck leaving at a fixed time.
script.title: One: a fixed rhythm, twice a day

script.say:
The second mechanism is the test.
Milk is paid for by its quality, and for most of Amul's history, quality meant fat. A litre with more fat is worth more. So the fat reading is the money.
The old method was called the Gerber test. You put sulphuric acid into a thin glass tube called a butyrometer. You add a measured amount of milk, then a little amyl alcohol. You seal it, shake it, spin it in a centrifuge for five minutes, and read the fat off a scale on the glass. It works. But it is slow, it uses acid, and at a busy counter with a few hundred members, it takes time.
So the dairy board worked with a Danish manufacturer on a small electronic tester for village use. It reads fat from the way light scatters through milk, and shows the number on a display. Today, many societies use an automatic milk collection unit. The weighing scale and the milk analyser are joined to a small computer. The member's number goes in. The machines capture the weight and the fat. The rate comes from a chart the union sends. The slip prints.
In the older counters, the result itself rode on the rhythm. The handbook describes the truck crew bringing back the fat slip of the previous shift, along with the clean cans. The answer arrived on schedule, with the truck, not when someone remembered to send it.
Here is the detail I find most important. The handbook says test results are recorded against a sample number, not a name, so the tester does not know whose milk he is testing. And if a member doubts a reading, she can ask for a retest before the samples are thrown away.
The handbook also notes what happened when electronic testers and collection units arrived. Member participation and trust grew.
Think about why. The test is fair, yes. But more than that, it is seen to be fair, by the person whose money depends on it, at the moment it happens. There is nothing to argue about later, because nothing was decided out of sight.
script.sees: PIP: PIP. A sample poured into a small beaker. Close-up of a glass butyrometer and a centrifuge. An electronic milk analyser display. An automatic collection unit at a counter, slip printing.
script.title: Two: the test, in front of the farmer

script.say:
The third mechanism is the record.
Every pour is written in two places. Once in the society's purchase register. And once in the member's own card or passbook, which she keeps. Where the counter is computerised, she also gets the printed slip. Date. Morning or evening. Cow or buffalo. Her member number. Weight. Fat. Rate. Amount.
So the work lives in a place both sides can see. Not in the secretary's memory. Not in a diary in a drawer. On a piece of paper in the farmer's hand, and in a register the auditor will check.
The newer systems go further. A dairy board presentation on collection software describes a digital passbook and a text-message service, so a farmer can check her quantity, her quality, today's price and her balance due, without asking anyone.
This is the first of my six questions. Where does the work live? Here, it lives on the slip and in the passbook.
It also answers the second question. How can anyone see the state of the work? The farmer sees it before she leaves the window. Litres, fat, rate, amount. If something is wrong, she knows in a minute, not at the end of the month.
Compare that with a supplier in your city waiting for his payment. He does not know what you have recorded against his name. He finds out when the money arrives, or does not. So he calls. And the call comes to you.
script.sees: PIP: PIP. GFX-05: the anatomy of the slip, each field lit in turn: date, shift, type of milk, member number, litres, fat, rate, amount. Then a handwritten passbook page with invented entries.
script.title: Three: the record the farmer carries home

script.say:
The fourth mechanism is the payment day.
I want to be exact here, because this part is often told loosely. The payment cycle at a village society is not the same everywhere, and it has changed over time.
The dairy board's handbook says a society pays its members daily, weekly or every ten days, as its elected managing committee decides. The same handbook says the union pays each society through the bank at a regular interval, weekly or every ten days. That interval is generally not changed, and it is the same for all societies. A government note in 2016 described the sector's cycles as weekly and ten-day. And in 2021, the managing director of the Kaira union wrote that each society is paid once in ten days.
So the cycle varies. What does not vary is that it is fixed, and known in advance.
The price is fixed in the same way. It is set per kilogram of fat, from the union's chart, not by the secretary. The federation reported paying 337 rupees per kilogram of fat in 2009 to 2010, and 765 rupees in 2019 to 2020. The farmer does not negotiate that number at the window. She checks it.
Since the end of 2016, payments have also moved into farmers' bank accounts.
At the end of the year, there is one more payment. Part of the society's surplus goes back to members as a bonus, in proportion to the milk each one supplied.
That is the third of my six questions. What is the feedback loop? Here, it runs on a timetable. Every shift, the slip. Every cycle, the money. Every month, the committee meets. Every year, the bonus and the audit.
A farmer does not need to ask when she will be paid. A secretary does not need to decide when to pay. A chairman does not need to approve each payment. The calendar decides.
script.sees: PIP: PIP. GFX-06: a calendar strip with three versions side by side, labelled daily, weekly and every ten days, each with its payment days marked in yellow.
script.title: Four: payment on a known day

script.say:
The fifth mechanism is the structure, and it is simpler than it sounds.
At the bottom is the village society, owned by its members. In the middle is the district union, owned by the societies. At the top is the state federation, formed by the unions. In Gujarat, that federation is GCMMF, set up in 1973, which sells under the Amul brand. Members elect the leaders at each level. Professional managers answer to those leaders.
Each tier does only what it is best placed to do. The village receives, tests, records and pays. The union buys all of the societies' milk, processes it, and supplies feed, vets and breeding services. The federation sells, under one name.
This answers my fourth question. How are errors caught before they travel? At the society, after each shift, the whole collection is sampled and tested again as one, which the handbook calls the general test. At the union, the milk is tested again at the dock. An auditor checks that every member has a passbook and that every pour is entered.
And since the 1990s, the Kaira union has chilled milk at the society itself, below four degrees within one to two hours of milking, so quality does not slip on the road. By 2016 to 2017, it had a bulk milk cooler in every one of its 1,202 village societies. Its tankers now carry sealed automatic samplers, so each society's sample is drawn by a machine, not a hand.
And it answers my fifth question. What happens when the owner is away? At the village counter, there is no owner. The committee is elected and unpaid. The secretary is paid to run the counter. The rate chart comes from the union. The rule is the same in Anand as in a village two hundred kilometres away. Nobody needs to be present for it to be kept.
script.sees: PIP: PIP. GFX-07: the three-tier diagram, with the village society repeated many times along the base, the district union above, the state federation at the top. Then a bulk milk cooler at a society, and a tanker on a highway.
script.title: Five: one rule, the same in every village

script.say:
Notice what the counter does not need.
It does not need the chairman to approve each payment. It does not need a call from Anand to open on time. It does not need the secretary to be a good judge of character, or the farmer to trust him personally. It does not need anyone to remember who brought what last Tuesday.
All of that has been moved out of people's heads, and into the rhythm, the test, the slip and the cycle. What is left for people is the work itself. Pouring, testing, loading, paying.
That is the difference between a system and a set of good people. Good people get tired. They go on leave. They leave. A rhythm does not.
Even the best-known person in this story eventually left, and not happily. I will come to that. The counters did not notice. They opened the next morning, at the same time.
script.sees: PIP: PIP. Palak's hand sketching the counter on paper: a box for the window, four arrows out of it labelled rhythm, test, record, day.
script.title: What the counter does not need

script.say:
Every system looks good on a normal Tuesday. The real question is what happens when something breaks. A flood of supply. A collapse in demand. A crisis nobody planned for.
Amul has been tested more than once. I want to show you three tests. The first, in the 1950s, was too much milk. The second, from 1970, was scale, whether the counter could be copied across India. The third was March 2020.
script.sees: FULL: FULL. Palak to camera.
script.title: Every system meets a bad year

script.say:
Buffaloes give about two and a half times as much milk in winter as in summer. By 1953, the Bombay scheme could not take the extra winter milk. Farmers were once again selling their surplus to middlemen, at low rates.
This mattered for the whole design. The farmer pours twice a day because the society will take all of her milk. If the society cannot take it in winter, the rhythm breaks, and the contractors come back.
The union's answer was a factory. A plant to turn surplus milk into milk powder and butter, costing about fifty lakh rupees. President Rajendra Prasad laid its foundation stone in November 1954. Prime Minister Nehru opened it on the thirty-first of October 1955. The union describes it as the first plant to make these products from buffalo milk at commercial scale.
The lesson is quiet, but important. When the promise at the counter came under pressure, they did not change the counter. They built capacity behind it, so the promise could hold.
script.sees: PIP: PIP. Archive images of the Anand dairy plant in the 1950s. GFX-09: a summer bar and a winter bar two and a half times taller.
script.title: Test one: the winter surplus

script.say:
The second test was scale.
On the thirty-first of October 1964, Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri came to Anand to open the union's cattle feed plant. He spent a night with farmers in the district. Then he asked Kurien to repeat the Anand model across the country. The National Dairy Development Board was set up at Anand in 1965. Operation Flood began in 1970.
What travelled was not a brand. It was the counter. A village society, a district union, a state federation, and the same routine at the bottom. Collect twice a day. Test. Record. Pay.
By the end of the first phase, in 1981, the programme had formed 13,270 village dairy cooperatives, covering about seventeen and a half lakh farm families. By the end of the third phase, the count was 72,744 cooperatives and about 93 lakh families. Those are the dairy board's own figures.
A rule that only works because one good person is watching cannot be copied seventy-two thousand times. A rule that is the same at every counter can.
script.sees: PIP: PIP. Archive photograph of Lal Bahadur Shastri. GFX-10: a map of India, milk sheds appearing phase by phase, with two counters: 13,270 societies, then 72,744.
script.title: Test two: copying the counter across India

script.say:
The third test is the one I find most striking.
India's lockdown began on the twenty-fifth of March 2020. For three days, Amul's sales rose as people stocked up. On the fourth day, they fell by about thirty percent. Hotels, sweet shops and restaurants shut. Many smaller and private dairies stopped buying milk.
Think about what that means at the village counter. A farmer still has buffaloes to milk, twice a day. If nobody buys, the milk is lost, and so is the month's income.
Amul did not stop collecting. Its managing director said in April 2020 that it was taking ten to fifteen percent more milk than usual, because the smaller dairies had closed. He said it was still paying forty-two rupees a litre for buffalo milk at six percent fat, and thirty-one rupees for cow milk at three and a half percent fat. The extra milk went into butter and milk powder, which keep for a year or two.
At its annual meeting that July, the federation said the Gujarat unions had procured an additional 35 lakh litres a day during the lockdown, giving about 800 crore rupees extra to rural milk producers. In June, the managing director said Amul had put about 9,000 crore rupees into the rural economy, in Gujarat and the other states where it works.
Why could it do this? Not only because people made brave decisions in a boardroom, though they did. It was because the counter already worked on a rhythm everyone knew. The society takes the milk. The test is done in front of you. The rate comes from the chart. The money comes on the known day. Nothing about that had to be invented in a crisis. It only had to keep going.
script.sees: PIP: PIP. Empty Indian streets in the 2020 lockdown. A milk tanker moving on an empty road. Butter blocks and milk powder bags in a store. GFX-11: one line for sales dipping, one for procurement rising.
script.title: Test three: March 2020

script.say: So, my sixth question. What happened when it broke? Demand broke. The counter did not. Morning and evening, the windows opened, the milk was tested, the slips printed, and the payments followed on the cycle.
script.sees: FULL: FULL. Palak to camera.
script.title: What the test showed

script.say:
Before I draw lessons, let me be honest about the limits.
Amul is not a forty-person firm. It is a federation of cooperatives, owned by its own suppliers. In its early years, the state bought its milk on contract at stable prices. Operation Flood was funded with donated milk powder and World Bank loans. Its boards are elected, and like many cooperatives in India, it has a political life. Chairmanships have been contested. Kurien himself resigned as chairman of the federation in March 2006, ahead of a no-confidence motion by his own board. Operation Flood also had serious critics, who questioned who gained most from it.
And yet the counters kept opening after 2006, morning and evening, as before.
You cannot copy a federation. You should not try.
But you can copy the counter. Because the counter is the place where your business meets a supplier, a worker or a customer. And that moment either needs you, or it does not.
Here are four things I take from Anand.
script.sees: FULL: FULL. Palak to camera.
script.title: Where the comparison stops

script.say:
First. A fixed rhythm removes the need to chase.
The farmer does not ask when collection opens. It opens at the same time every day.
In your firm, pick the one thing you chase most. For many owners, it is dispatch. Give it a time. Dispatch closes at four. Whatever is packed, checked and billed by four goes today. Whatever is not goes tomorrow, and the sheet shows why. Then give the week a rhythm. On Monday, everyone gets their list. On Friday, everyone sees their score.
Once the time is fixed, you stop being the alarm clock. You no longer walk to the floor at six in the evening to ask, "ho gaya?" Four o'clock has already answered.
script.sees: FULL: FULL. Palak to camera. Brief cutaway to a dispatch bay with cartons stacked.
script.title: Lesson one: a fixed rhythm removes the need to chase

script.say:
Second. A test done in front of the person removes the argument.
At the counter, the farmer watches her milk being tested. If she doubts it, she asks for a retest, there and then. Nobody argues a week later.
Most disputes in our firms come from a check done out of sight. The customer says the lot was short. The supervisor says it was full. Nobody can show it. So move the check to where both sides can see it. Weigh the lot with the driver present, and photograph the reading. Read the quote back to the client on the call, line by line, before you send it. Count the stock with the store keeper and the accountant together, on a fixed date each month.
The aim is not to catch anyone. The aim is to settle the question at the moment it is cheapest to settle.
script.sees: FULL: FULL. Palak to camera. Brief cutaway to goods being weighed with a driver present.
script.title: Lesson two: a test done in front of the person removes the argument

script.say:
Third. A visible record settles the payment.
The farmer leaves with a slip. Litres, fat, rate, amount. When the money comes, she checks it against her own record.
Think of your suppliers, your contract workers, your clients. What do they hold in their hand after each transaction? Usually nothing. So they call. A simple record, shared at the moment of the work, changes that. A delivery note signed by both sides. A job card that shows the hours. A client file where the client can see what stage the work is at, and what is due from them.
When both sides hold the same record, the payment stops being a negotiation. It becomes a check.
script.sees: FULL: FULL. Palak to camera. Brief cutaway to a delivery note being signed by two hands.
script.title: Lesson three: a visible record settles the payment

script.say:
Fourth. The system grows because the rule at the smallest unit is the same everywhere.
Operation Flood did not copy Kurien. It copied the counter, more than seventy thousand times.
In a firm of forty, the smallest unit is one piece of work. One order. One quote. One client file. If each of those has a home, with a name, a date and a next step, then it does not matter whether the owner is at the desk, at a wedding, or on a plane. The rule holds.
So do not start with the whole firm. Start with one process. Make the rule at that counter the same every time. Run it for a month. Then copy it to the next process, and the next branch, without changing the rule.
That is how a small room in Samarkha became more than seventy thousand rooms across India. Not by finding seventy thousand remarkable people. By keeping one rule simple enough to repeat.
script.sees: FULL: FULL. Palak to camera. Brief cutaway to her hand writing a task with a name, a date and a next step.
script.title: Lesson four: the same rule at the smallest unit

script.say:
In my family's firm, VSP Consultants, we were the follow-up department for years. Every update, every payment question, every "is it done" came to one desk. What changed it was not working harder. It was giving the work a home, a fixed rhythm, and a record everyone could see. [your own line]
This is the work I do now, at Venture Drafters. I sit with an owner, find the one process that comes through them most often, and design its counter: the rhythm, the check and the record. We set it up on your own sheet, train your team, and manage it with you.
Four things, then. A fixed rhythm, so nobody has to chase. A check done in front of the person, so nobody has to argue. A record both sides can see, so the payment settles itself. And one rule, the same at the smallest counter, so the firm can grow without the owner in every room.
A farmer in Anand does not need to chase her payment. Your supplier should not need to either. And neither should you.
If you want to see how this looks for your business, book a 30-minute call. The link is in the description.
script.sees: FULL: FULL. Palak to camera.
script.title: What I do now

script.say: This was Built to Run. Every figure in this episode, and its source, is listed in the description. Thank you for watching.

snapshot.notes:
Built to Run: Stories, episode 04: Amul. Twice a day, every day, for 3.6 million people.. Source: Marketing/case-studies/04-amul.md (script, b-roll list, slide outline, fact sheet, sources, cut-downs). Fortnightly Monday slot 2026-12-21, 11:00.

Do not claim (from the fact sheet):
- That Kurien founded Amul. The farmers and Tribhuvandas Patel founded and registered the union in 1946; Kurien arrived in May 1949.
- "247 litres" as the first day's collection. The union's own pages say about 250 litres a day in June 1948. Use "about 250".
- That every society pays daily, or that Amul pays "every ten days" everywhere. The cycle varies by society and period; say "on a fixed cycle, set in advance".
- "Rs 200 crore paid daily to farmers" as evidence of a daily payment cycle. It is an aggregate value of milk bought, not a payment schedule.
- That farmers receive 80 to 85 percent of the consumer rupee, as a verified fact. It is a figure GCMMF's managing director has repeated; it is the company's own claim and has not been independently checked here.
- Rs 1 lakh crore as GCMMF's turnover. That is the wider Amul brand figure; GCMMF's own 2025-26 turnover is Rs 73,450 crore.
- That Operation Flood alone made India the world's largest milk producer. The causal link is debated.
- The story that Manthan was funded by farmers contributing two rupees each, unless separately verified.
- Any reason for Kurien's 2006 exit beyond the public record: he resigned ahead of a no-confidence motion and cited a High Court order.
- Anecdotes about Kurien's personal habits (for example, that he did not drink milk). Not verified here.
- "Within a month I left the government creamery to join the Kaira Cooperative" as the sequel to Tribhuvandas Patel's request. In the book it follows an astrologer's prediction, and the Kaira union says Kurien got his relieving order at the end of 1949.
- Rs 9,000 crore as the amount paid "over those months" of the lockdown. The source gives no period.
- A fortnightly payment cycle for farmers. No source found.
- "India's largest" or "No. 1" in Palak's own voice. Use the sourced numbers instead.

passthrough.openQuestions:
1. Payment cycle: I could verify daily, weekly and ten-day cycles (NDDB handbook; Kaira union, 2021), but not a fortnightly cycle from a source I could read. The script says "fixed and known in advance" and gives the range. If you want a current figure, one call to a Gujarat union's procurement office would settle it.
2. Which scale figure to use: April 2026 reports give about 31 million litres a day; April 2025 gives 300 lakh. The script says "about 3 crore litres a day". The 18,600 villages figure is from a 2025 news report (Medium); older GCMMF decks give 18,549 societies.
3. I Too Had a Dream: the two Kurien lines are taken from a 2024 newspaper column that quotes the book. Please check them against your copy, with page numbers, before recording.
4. Sensitivity: Kurien's 2006 exit and later board politics involve living people and political parties. The script states only the public record and names no politician. Keep it that way.
5. The cold open is a composite scene, captioned as such. If you can film at a dairy cooperative society near Indore, the opening becomes real footage; it needs written permission and no member faces or numbers on screen.
6. Web research ran out of search budget before I could confirm a current count of automatic collection units and bulk coolers across all GCMMF unions, or the Manthan funding story. Neither is used in the script.

### Fact-check log, 30 October 2026

**Confirmed**
- 4 January 1946 Samarkha meeting, 14 December 1946 registration, 15-day strike, June 1948 start, 432 farmers and 5,000 litres by end 1948 (Kaira Union history page, amuldairy.com/history.php).
- Kurien arrived 13 May 1949; roles and years (amuldairy.com/dr_kurien.php).
- "Excruciatingly unexciting and conservative" is in I Too Had a Dream (Google Books phrase search, Roli Books edition; page number not retrieved).
- Lockdown: 35 lakh litres a day, about Rs 800 crore extra (Asian Age, DeshGujarat); 10 to 15 percent more milk, Rs 42 and Rs 31 prices, 30 percent fall (Just Food).
- Rs 337 to Rs 765 per kg fat (Asian Age, DeshGujarat).
- Rs 73,450 crore, 36 lakh farmers, about 31 million litres a day (Free Press Journal, Dairy Business MEA); 18 unions, 18,600 villages (Storyboard18, FY25).
- Payment: daily, weekly or ten-day (NDDB handbook p. 61); GCMMF said weekly in November 2016 (DeshGujarat).

**Changed**
- Script said Kurien wrote "Within a month I left..." Now quotes "excruciatingly unexciting and conservative". In the book the first line follows an astrologer's prediction, so the lead-in misled.
- Script said Rs 9,000 crore was paid "over those months". Now says the managing director said Amul had put about Rs 9,000 crore into the rural economy (The Week gives no period).
- Essay and script said Rs 800 crore "worth" to producers. Now "extra to rural milk producers" (Asian Age).
- Confidence raised to High: fat price and lockdown rows.

**Still unverified**
- Fortnightly farmer payment cycle: none found in NDDB, Kaira union, GCMMF or PIB sources.
- 18,600 villages for 2026: no April 2026 report gives a count.
- Book page numbers: previews blocked.
- GCMMF's own July 2020 press release PDF: 403 error.
