tags: mcdonald's. the business the brothers drew in chalk.

script.say:
It is late at night in San Bernardino, California. The year is 1952, or early 1953. Behind a family house there is a tennis court. On it, two brothers are drawing a kitchen in chalk.
There is no kitchen. There is no food. Their crew has come over after closing time. One man stands where a grill will be and turns patties that are not there. Another walks to a fry station and back. A third reaches for buns from a rack that exists only as a line on the ground.
Each time someone takes a step too many, the brothers rub out a line and draw it again. They are designing the work before anyone designs the building.
This is how the best-known history of the company tells it. By three in the morning the layout is right. The draftsman will copy it tomorrow. That night, it rains. The red chalk runs off the court in streaks.
The drawing is gone. What the brothers learned by walking it is not. That kitchen will be copied in towns they will never visit, by people they will never meet.
So here is the question for today. What does it take for a business to work the same way when the owner is not in the room?
This is Built to Run. Stories of businesses that run on systems, not on memory.
script.sees: VO: Night. An empty hard court under one floodlight; a hand draws a long chalk line; feet step between chalk boxes; rain begins to fall and the lines run. Title card at the end: "Built to Run. Episode 9."
script.title: The tennis court at night

script.say:
Let me go back twelve years before that night.
In 1940, Richard and Maurice McDonald open a drive-in in San Bernardino. People call them Dick and Mac. The building is small and eight-sided. There are no seats inside. Cars pull into the lot, and carhops take the order at the car window and bring the food out on a tray.
On a weekend evening there can be 125 cars in that lot. About twenty carhops run between them. The menu has about twenty-five items, most of them barbecue.
And it works. By the middle of the 1940s the drive-in sells more than 200,000 dollars a year. The two brothers share about 50,000 dollars of profit.
Those figures come from John Love's history of the company, written with McDonald's cooperation. I rely on it for most of the early story, and I will tell you where it disagrees with the version you may have seen in a film.
So this is not a story about a business in trouble. It is a story about a business that was doing well, run by two owners who could see what it cost them to keep it that way.
script.sees: FULL: A, Palak at her desk. Cut to PIP over archive drive-in footage at "In 1940".
script.title: A drive-in that worked

script.say:
Here is what they could see.
The carhops did not stay. They left for better pay, and every new one had to be taught again. Plates and glasses broke, or went home with customers. The crowd in the lot was mostly teenagers, and families stayed away.
None of these problems was dramatic. Each one was small. And each one landed on the brothers.
I think every owner watching knows this feeling. The business is good. The customers are happy. And yet you are the one who trains the new person. You are the one who notices the missing stock. You are the one who walks over at seven in the evening and asks the question owners across India ask every day: "ho gaya?"
Then the brothers did something useful. They sat down with three years of their own receipts. And they found that about eighty percent of their sales were hamburgers.
They were running a barbecue drive-in with twenty-five items. Their customers were buying a hamburger.
That gap, between the business you run and the business your customers buy, is where most of an owner's tiredness comes from. Every extra item is something to train, stock, check and chase.
script.sees: PIP: Old receipts sorted by hand; GFX-01 timeline begins at 1940.
script.title: What the brothers could see

script.say:
In the autumn of 1948, the brothers close the drive-in. Not for a week. For three months.
They let the carhops go. They decide to rebuild the whole operation around the one thing customers actually come for.
I want to stay on this for a moment, because it is the hardest part of the story for an owner to copy. Most of us redesign while we run. We add a new form on top of the old habit. We hire one more person to follow up. We buy software and keep the old register, just in case.
The brothers stopped. They gave themselves room to design the work before they did it again.
Think about what that meant in 1948. They had a business that paid them well. Their staff depended on it. Their customers came every weekend. There was no certainty it would come back. They did it because their own receipts had shown them something. The old design would always need them standing in the middle of it. They wanted a design that needed them less.
You do not have to close your firm for three months. But you do need a few protected hours where you are not running the work, only looking at it.
And the first thing the brothers designed was not a building, or a sign, or an advertisement. It was the menu.
script.sees: FULL: First two lines to camera, then cut to PIP over a "Closed" sign turned on a glass door.
script.title: Closing a business that works

script.say:
The menu goes from about twenty-five items to nine. Hamburgers. Cheeseburgers. Drinks. A few things more.
The hamburger goes from thirty cents to fifteen. And every hamburger comes with the same condiments. No choices.
The plates and glasses go. Food comes in paper bags, paper wrappers and paper cups. The customer walks up to a window and collects the order.
Now look at what each choice removes.
The short menu removes decisions at the grill. A cook who makes nine things makes them the same way every time.
The fixed condiments remove the special order. No one has to remember that the third car wanted no onion.
The paper removes the dishwasher. A whole job, gone. And with it, the cost of every broken plate.
Self-service removes the carhop, the one role the brothers could never keep filled.
A note on the price, too. Halving the price only works if the cost of making each burger falls with it. Fewer items. Less waste. No dishwasher. No carhops. The low price was a result of the design, not a bet on crowds alone.
None of this is about speed for its own sake. Each choice takes away a place where the work could vary. When the work cannot vary much, a new person can do it well. That is the quiet idea under everything that follows.
script.sees: PIP: GFX-02, a menu board counting down from 25 items to 9. Then a paper bag, a wrapper and a paper cup set down on a counter.
script.title: Mechanism one: the short menu

script.say:
Then they rebuild the kitchen around the work.
Two grills, each six feet long, replace a standard three-foot grill. Dick McDonald designs a steel turntable that holds twenty-four buns, so one person can dress them in a row. A local machinist builds a hand pump that puts the same measure of ketchup and mustard on every bun.
The crew is split into stations. Three on the grill. Two on shakes. Two on fries. Two dressing buns. Three at the counter. Each person has one job, and a fixed place to do it.
They call it the Speedee Service System. The target is to hand over an order in thirty seconds or less.
And here is the part people leave out. When they reopen, business falls to about a fifth of what it was. It takes about six months to come back. By 1951 the restaurant takes 277,000 dollars, nearly forty percent more than the old drive-in.
Six months of worse numbers. Every owner who has changed a working process knows those months. The brothers held their nerve.
Now, the tennis court. You will often hear that the chalk drawing happened in 1948. The film The Founder shows it that way. Love's history, and the architectural historian Alan Hess, place it a few years later, in 1952 and 1953. By then the brothers wanted a new building that other people could copy. So before the architect drew a single wall, they drew the kitchen on the court and walked the crew through it. The building, with its golden arches, was designed around that kitchen.
That is the order. The work first. The building second.
script.sees: PIP: GFX-03, the station diagram with twelve figures. Grill, fries, shake mixer. A phone stopwatch running to thirty seconds.
script.title: Mechanism two: the kitchen drawn around the steps

script.say:
The brothers did sell franchises themselves, before anyone else came along.
Each buyer received a manual of fifteen pages, a set of building plans, the right to the name, and one week of training in San Bernardino.
After that, as Love puts it, they could run their stores as they chose. And most did.
Prices differed from town to town. Some added items to the menu. One owner reshaped the arches into a point and gave the place a different name. Few of them were as clean as the original. Few sold as much.
This is worth noticing. The brothers had designed the work beautifully. In their own restaurant, under their own eyes, it ran to the second. But the design lived where they lived. Nobody was checking the other kitchens. Nobody found out when something slipped, until it showed in the sales.
That is the owner's problem in one sentence. The system worked where the owner could see it. Away from the owner, it drifted.
In the words I use with owners, the brothers were still the feedback loop. And a feedback loop that is one person's eyes cannot travel.
script.sees: FULL: First line to camera, then cut to PIP over GFX: "15 pages. Plans. The name. One week of training."
script.title: The gap the brothers left

script.say:
In 1954 a salesman named Ray Kroc notices something odd. He sells a milkshake machine called the Multimixer. One small restaurant in California keeps ordering more of them. In Love's account, the order is for their ninth and tenth.
He flies out to see why. At lunch he finds queues at the windows, and orders handed over in about fifteen seconds.
He asks the brothers for the right to sell franchises across the country, and they agree. The terms are modest. A franchise costs 950 dollars. The franchisee pays 1.9 percent of sales as a service fee, and half a percent of that goes to the brothers.
On 15 April 1955, Kroc opens his own restaurant in Des Plaines, Illinois, as a model for buyers to visit. McDonald's still dates its founding to that day.
Then he makes a decision that matters more than any fee. Other chains at the time sell whole territories. One buyer pays a large sum and gets a city, or a state. Kroc refuses. He sells one store at a time.
His reason, as Love records it, is control. If a man owns the territory, he owns the business in that area, and he can ignore the standard. If a man owns one store and wants a second, he has to earn it.
The unit of the franchise is the unit of the standard. Keep that idea. It comes back.
script.sees: PIP: A milkshake spindle mixer; the Des Plaines museum exterior; GFX-06, territory against single store.
script.title: Mechanism three: one store at a time

script.say:
The person who writes the standard down is Fred Turner. He starts as one of the first grill men at Des Plaines. Within months he is writing manuals for franchisees.
His first is fifteen pages, typed and copied. The next is thirty-eight. In 1958 he produces a printed, bound manual of seventy-five pages.
Listen to the level of detail.
A quarter of an ounce of onion on each patty. French fries cut nine thirty-seconds of an inch thick. Cooking times. Temperature settings. Any meat or potatoes held more than ten minutes in the serving bin are thrown away. The grill man lays the patties from left to right, six rows of six, and turns the third row first.
About ten pages are forms. Inventory. Cash. Staff schedules.
And the opening line, as Love quotes it: "Herein outlined is the successful method."
Notice what kind of document this is. It is not a policy. It does not say "maintain high standards". It says nine thirty-seconds of an inch. A young man on his first day can read it and do the step. So can a manager in another state who has never met Kroc.
That is where the work lives at McDonald's. Not in the best cook's memory. On the page, and in the layout of the kitchen.
And look at the ten-minute rule again. It does two jobs. It catches an error before it reaches the customer. And it makes the state of the work visible. Anyone can look at the bin and the clock and see whether the rule is being kept.
script.sees: PIP: GFX-07, page counter 15, then 38, then 75. GFX-08, the specification card. A ring binder opened on a desk; a ruler against a cut potato stick.
script.title: Mechanism four: the manual

script.say:
A manual is only half of it. Someone has to check.
Turner builds an inspection report. The first version is seven pages, single-spaced. Cleanliness. Food quality. Cooking times and temperatures. How long service takes.
Kroc will not read seven pages. So Turner puts a letter grade, A to F, in the top right corner.
This is how QSC begins. Quality, service, cleanliness. In the middle of the 1960s Kroc adds a V, for value.
One detail I like. Operators were never formally graded on value, because franchisees set their own prices. You grade what the operator controls.
And the grade has a consequence. By the middle of the 1960s it decides whether an operator may open another store. By the 1990s, Love writes, more than 330 field consultants each look after about twenty-one restaurants, and visit several times a year. A B is the minimum to grow.
So here is the feedback loop. The owner does not have to ask. A person who is not the owner walks into the kitchen, times the service, looks at the bin, checks the floor, and writes a grade anyone can read.
Think about what the grade does for Kroc. He cannot stand in hundreds of kitchens. He can read hundreds of letters. The grade turns a seven-page visit into one mark a busy owner can act on. That is the whole job of a report.
That is a standard a stranger can check.
script.sees: PIP: GFX-09, an inspection report with a letter grade in the top right corner; the letters Q, S, C appear, V greyed. A clipboard ticked in a kitchen.
script.title: Mechanism five: the grade in the corner

script.say:
In February 1961 the company opens a school in the basement of a new restaurant in Elk Grove Village, near Chicago. Fifteen people in the first class. They call it Hamburger University.
The first course runs two weeks. Potato varieties. The meat formula. How each machine works, taught on cut-away models. By 2011 the company says more than 275,000 people have graduated, taught in twenty-eight languages.
Notice why the school matters. A manual tells you what to do. Training makes sure the person at the grill has seen it done, and has done it, before a customer is waiting. The manual and the school are one design. The step, written down. And the step, practised.
In the same year, 1961, Kroc buys out the brothers for 2.7 million dollars. How that sale was handled, and how the brothers felt about it, is still argued over. I am not going to take a side.
One more layer, briefly. From 1956, Kroc's finance man, Harry Sonneborn, leased the land under each restaurant and rented it on to the franchisee at a markup. It gave McDonald's an income that did not depend on fees. It is the financial system under the operating system. It matters to McDonald's. It does not matter to your firm.
script.sees: PIP: Hamburger University photographs from the company press library; GFX-10, two layers, the operating system above and the real estate below.
script.title: Hamburger University, and the system underneath

script.say:
So before we go to India, the five questions.
Where does the work live? On the page, and in the layout. How can anyone see its state? The thirty-second target, the ten-minute bin, the grade in the corner. What is the feedback loop? The consultant's visit, and a grade that decides the next store. How are errors caught? Fixed portions, discard times, inspections.
And what happens when the owner is away? At McDonald's the owner is always away. Kroc never met most of the people running his kitchens.
Notice what is missing from that list. Kroc standing at the counter. The brothers watching the grill. The design does not need the owner in the kitchen. It needs the owner at the design, and at the review.
script.sees: PIP: GFX-15, the six questions card, first five rows filling in.
script.title: Five answers so far

script.say:
Now the test. And I want to take it somewhere close to home.
McDonald's opens in India in October 1996, at Basant Lok in Vasant Vihar, New Delhi. A restaurant at Bandra in Mumbai follows the same month.
Two Indian partners run it. In the north and east, Connaught Plaza Restaurants, a joint venture led by Vikram Bakshi. In the west and south, Hardcastle Restaurants, led by Amit Jatia. Jatia, by his own account, is a vegetarian running a family industrial business when a friend suggests the partnership. He goes on to train at Hamburger University.
The menu is redesigned for India. No beef. No pork. It is the first McDonald's to serve neither. There is a wide vegetarian range.
And the kitchen is redesigned too. Vegetarian and non-vegetarian food are kept apart all the way from the processing plant to the restaurant kitchen. That is not a line on a poster. It is a line on the floor, the way the brothers drew theirs.
But the part that interests me most is the timing. The company says it spent six years building the supply chain before the first restaurant opened. Six years of work before one rupee of sales.
script.sees: FULL: First two lines to camera, then cut to PIP over Delhi and Mumbai street footage, GFX-11 India map, and two cutting boards, one green and one red.
script.title: Six years before the first burger

script.say:
Take lettuce. When McDonald's arrives, iceberg lettuce is imported. In India it grows in a window of about sixty days a year.
By its own account, the company spends three years finding the right places to grow it. It trains five to six hundred farmers. It writes farming process manuals in several languages. And it audits the farms against the standard.
Listen to that again. Process manuals, and audits. It is Fred Turner's 1958 manual, taken to a farm.
Potatoes take longer. Until 2007, the fries are imported. Work on a suitable potato in Gujarat begins in 2004. The first Indian-grown fry potato arrives in 2007. It takes about six more years before every order of fries uses Indian potatoes.
And none of it works without cold. In 1997 the company brings in trucks with three zones. Frozen, at minus eighteen. Chilled, at one to four degrees. And dry. Where a restaurant has no proper loading dock, the cases are covered with thermal blankets to hold their temperature for the fifteen or twenty minutes from truck to kitchen.
The early suppliers are Indian companies, several in partnership with McDonald's global vendors. Patties from Taloja. Cheese from Baramati. Lettuce from Talegaon. A cold-chain distributor serving the restaurants.
This is the India version of the chalk drawing. Before they served a single customer, they designed the work all the way back to the farm.
script.sees: PIP: Lettuce fields and farmers; a potato harvest; a cold store with pallets; GFX-13, a truck in cross-section with three zones; GFX-12, the India timeline.
script.title: Lettuce, potatoes and a truck with three temperatures

script.say:
Every system is tested. In north and east India, the test was a dispute between partners. I will tell it only as the public record does, because the people involved are living, and the matter is settled.
In 2013 McDonald's voted against Vikram Bakshi's re-election as managing director of Connaught Plaza Restaurants, the fifty-fifty joint venture. A long legal dispute followed.
From June 2017, 43 of the joint venture's Delhi restaurants were shut after their eating-house licences expired. In July 2017 the National Company Law Tribunal reinstated Bakshi as managing director. In August 2017 McDonald's India ended the franchise agreements for all 169 restaurants, citing unpaid royalties and other obligations. The joint venture disputed that. In December 2017 the logistics partner said it would stop supplies, and about eighty restaurants faced closure.
In May 2019 the two sides settled out of court, and McDonald's bought Bakshi's stake.
script.sees: FULL: First paragraph to camera, then cut to PIP over GFX-14, the dispute timeline, dates and facts only.
script.title: The test: when the partnership broke

script.say:
I want to draw two things from this. Neither is a judgement on any person.
First, look at what failed. The restaurants did not close because anyone forgot how to make a burger. The manual was still there. They closed when licences lapsed, and others faced closure when the cold chain stopped. The parts of the system that depend on a working relationship failed first.
Second, look at how the recovery began. With the settlement, McDonald's closed the north and east restaurants temporarily, to reopen over about two weeks. The reason it gave was a comprehensive assessment of operational protocols and employee training. It began with a review of how the work was done and how people were trained.
There is a lesson for an owner even here. Your system includes your suppliers, your licences and your partners. A manual cannot protect you from a broken relationship. What it can do is show you, quickly, where the break is.
That is question six. What happened when it broke? The first step back was a review of the standard.
script.sees: FULL:
script.title: What failed first, and what came back first

script.say:
Now let me speak to you directly, as the owner of a business of fifteen or a hundred people.
First, the honest limit. McDonald's today has more than 45,000 restaurants, most of them run by franchisees. It owns land. It spent six years and a great deal of capital in India before it sold a burger. Your firm will do none of that, and it does not need to.
I also want to be careful. I am not saying a forty-person firm should behave like a franchise. Your clients know you. Your team knows you. That is a strength. The point is only that what you know should not live in you alone.
Michael Gerber's book The E-Myth Revisited uses McDonald's as its central example of a business designed as a prototype, built to be repeated by people who are not the founder. That is the useful idea. Not the size. The manual and the standard.
So here are four things I take from this story.
script.sees: FULL:
script.title: Where the comparison stops

script.say:
One. Design the work before you buy the building.
The brothers drew the kitchen before the architect drew the walls. In your firm, the building is the software, the new hire, the bigger office. Before any of those, take one process. An enquiry becoming a quote. An order becoming a dispatch. Draw it on paper. Every step, every handover, every person. Then walk it, the way the crew walked the tennis court.
And while you draw it, cut the menu. The brothers went from twenty-five items to nine, so each one could be made the same way every time. Many firms offer every client something slightly different. Five ways to quote. Three ways to confirm an order. Each variation is a place where the work depends on one person's memory. Cut it until it can be done the same way every time.
script.sees: FULL: A 3-second insert of K1, Palak's hand drawing boxes and arrows, at "Draw it on paper".
script.title: Lesson one: design the work, then cut the menu

script.say:
Two. Write the step so a new person can do it on day one.
Fred Turner did not write "cook the fries well". He wrote nine thirty-seconds of an inch, and ten minutes in the bin.
In your firm, that means the dispatch checklist says which documents go in the envelope, in which order, and who signs. The client file says what is due, on what date, and what the next step is. Work needs a home. A name, a date, a next step.
If your best person is the only one who knows how a quote is priced, the work lives in their memory. That is not their fault. It is a design that has not been done yet.
[your own line]
script.sees: FULL: A 3-second GLIMPSE of S1, a masked sheet with the owner, due date and next step columns in frame.
script.title: Lesson two: write the step for day one

script.say:
Three. A standard is something a stranger can check.
QSC worked because a consultant who had never met the operator could walk in and give a grade. That is the test I would put to any rule in your office.
If you wrote "follow up with clients promptly", nobody can check it. If you wrote "every enquiry gets a quote within two working days, and the sheet shows the date it went", anyone can check it. Your accountant can. Your son or daughter can. A new manager can, in the first week.
And grade what people control. McDonald's never graded value, because operators set the prices. Do not score your dispatch team on a delay the transporter caused.
Try it with one process this week. Write three rules for it. Then ask someone who does not do that work to check them on Friday. If they cannot tell whether a rule was kept, the rule needs rewriting, not the person.
script.sees: FULL:
script.title: Lesson three: a standard a stranger can check

script.say:
Four. The owner's job is the design and the Friday review, not the counter.
The brothers were brilliant at the counter. In their own restaurant, nothing slipped. But their licensees drifted, because the only loop was the brothers' own eyes. Kroc and Turner built something else. A manual. A visit. A grade. And a rule that the grade decides what happens next.
For a firm of forty people, that looks very ordinary. On Monday, the work is handed out, each item with a name, a date and a next step. On Friday, the score comes back. What was done. What is late. What is stuck. You read one screen. You stop being the follow-up department. You stop finding out last.
Start with one process. That is how the brothers started too. One menu. One kitchen. One tennis court.
script.sees: FULL: A 3-second GLIMPSE of S2, a masked dashboard with one amber row, at "You read one screen".
script.title: Lesson four: the design and the Friday review

script.say:
The brothers' chalk washed away in one night of rain. What lasted was what they learned by walking it. Where each step belongs. Who does it. How you know it was done.
I have spent a long time with this story, because it is so often told as a story about a salesman, or about a brand. To me it is a story about a manual and a grade. Two brothers designed the work. The people after them designed the loop.
In my family's firm, VSP Consultants, I learned this the slow way. The work lived in people's heads. The owner was the memory, the follow-up department and the feedback loop. So I designed our system on our own sheet. Where each piece of work lives, who has it, when it is due, and the score on Friday. The firm runs on it every day.
This is the work I do now, for owners of businesses with fifteen to a hundred people. We start with one process. We set it up on your own sheet, train your team on it, and keep it running. Your team still does the work. On the first call, I show you one live system, on a demo copy with invented data, so you can judge it for yourself.
If you want to see how this looks for your business, book a 30-minute call. The link is in the description.
Thank you for watching Built to Run.
script.sees: FULL: End card from 29:40: the Venture Drafters logo, "Book a 30-minute call", link in description.
script.title: What I do now

snapshot.notes:
Built to Run: Stories, episode 09: McDonald's. The business the brothers drew in chalk.. Source: Marketing/case-studies/09-mcdonalds.md (script, b-roll list, slide outline, fact sheet, sources, cut-downs). Fortnightly Monday slot 2027-03-01, 11:00.

Do not claim (from the fact sheet):
- That the brothers drew the kitchen on the tennis court in 1948. Love and Hess place it in 1952 to 1953; the 1948 date comes from the film *The Founder*.
- That Ray Kroc founded the first McDonald's, or that Des Plaines was the first McDonald's. It was Kroc's first.
- That Kroc cheated the brothers, or the "handshake royalty" story, as fact. The terms and feelings around the 1961 sale are disputed.
- "McDonald's is a real-estate company, not a burger company" as a present-day fact, or as Kroc's words. Love attributes a version of the line to Sonneborn speaking to analysts.
- That Hamburger University is "harder to get into than Harvard".
- That McDonald's India invested Rs 1,000 crore before launch. Westlife's figure is through suppliers over two decades.
- That McDonald's India has "never had a stock-out" or a fulfilment rate "higher than in developed markets". These are the company's own claims.
- That India was the first McDonald's with a vegetarian menu. The verifiable first is a menu without beef or pork.
- Any reason, motive or wrongdoing in the Connaught Plaza dispute beyond the court and company statements listed above.
- That each restaurant was checked against the standard before reopening in May 2019. The sources give only the stated reason: an assessment of operational protocols and employee training.
- That the Bandra restaurant opened exactly three days after Vasant Vihar. Only blog sources say so.
- Any original ownership split for Hardcastle Restaurants. Secondary sources describe a 1995 joint venture with McDonald's later converted to a master franchise; no primary source found.
- That Amit Jatia trained at Hamburger University before the 1996 opening. Business Today (2022) says only that he trained there.
- A current page count for the McDonald's operations manual.
- The *Outlook* figures for Dynamix Dairy's milk and cheese volumes, which appear garbled in the archived text.

passthrough.openQuestions:
1. **The tennis-court date.** The brief set it in 1948. John Love's history and Alan Hess's 1986 paper both place the chalk drawing in 1952 to 1953, for the new franchise building; 1948 comes from the film *The Founder*. The script uses 1952 and says so on camera. Please confirm you are happy to correct the popular version.
2. **Love's page and chapter references** were taken from a text of the revised edition. Check them against a physical copy before quoting page numbers anywhere public. Kroc's *Grinding It Out* was not consulted.
3. **Six years or three.** Westlife and McDonald's India say six years of supply-chain work before opening; a late-1990s *Outlook* report says supplier work began three years before. The script uses the company's six years. The exact day of the Bandra opening, and the original ownership structure of Hardcastle Restaurants, were not verified, so the script does not state them.
4. **Living people in Act 3.** Vikram Bakshi and Amit Jatia are living. The dispute section states only dated, reported facts and takes no side. Consider a brief legal read before publishing. If you prefer to avoid it, the brothers' drifting licensees (10:35) can serve as the test instead, with Act 3 shortened to the India supply chain.
5. **Company figures.** The restaurant count (45,356 at end of 2025) comes via Wikipedia from the 2025 annual report; check the 10-K. Westlife's Rs 1,000 crore and 99 percent fulfilment figures are self-reported; the script leaves them out.

### Fact-check log, 30 October 2026

**Confirmed**
- Restaurant count 45,356 and about 95 percent franchised: McDonald's 10-K for 2025.
- Six years of supply-chain work: Westlife AR 2014-15 letter; McDonald's India Farm to Fork.
- Lettuce wording (three-year research, 500 to 600 farmers, manuals, audits): Westlife AR 2014-15, p. 10. It is the company's own claim.
- Trucks in 1997, thermal blankets, potato dates 2004, 2007, about 2013: Westlife AR; Farm to Fork.

- Dispute dates, 169 outlets, 43 of 55 Delhi outlets, 80 outlets facing closure, December 2022 NCLAT: Scroll, AP, Deccan Chronicle, Business Today.
- Fries 9/32 inch equals 0.28 inch; 1958 manual: business-history pages.

**Changed**

- "Before opening, he goes through Hamburger University" now "He goes on to train there": Business Today 2022 gives no timing.
- Lettuce lines now say "by its own account": Westlife AR is the only source.
- "Each restaurant was checked against the standard" removed. Now: temporary closure, reopening over about two weeks, for an assessment of protocols and training: Reuters; Business Today 9 May 2019.
- "Cold chain stopped" closures now "others faced closure": Business Today, 26 December 2017.

**Still unverified**
- Love's rain, 3 a.m., ten-minute rule, onion weight, 15, 38 and 75 pages, QSC and 330 consultants: the book is lending-only and not searchable.

tags: zara. the shop that orders twice a week.

li.text:
I spent this week reading about Zara, and the detail that stayed with me was a clock.

In 2004, Harvard Business Review described the ordering deadlines in Zara's shops. In Spain and southern Europe, three in the afternoon on Wednesday and six in the evening on Saturday. A shop that missed Wednesday waited until Saturday.

As a designer, I find that more interesting than any technology the company bought later. A fixed clock is a design decision. It tells the factory when to cut, the warehouse when to load and the shop when to clear space. Nobody has to ask whether the order went. The day answers.

Most owners I meet place their main order when someone remembers. The quantity is last time's, plus a little extra. Then they spend the week asking whether it went.

The smallest change I know is to give that order two fixed days a week, and keep them.

If you run a trading or distribution business, which day does your main order go today?

script.say:
It is Wednesday afternoon in a clothes shop in Spain. The clock on the back wall says ten to three.
The manager walks the rails. A white shirt has sold out in medium. A dress has gone in two sizes. Three customers this week asked for a jacket in a darker colour, and the shop does not have it.
She types her order into a handheld device. The deadline is three o'clock. If she misses it, she waits until Saturday.
By Friday, a truck will bring what she asked for. Not a season's worth. A few pieces of each. Enough for the next few days. Then she will order again.
This happens in every shop of the company, twice a week, every week, at fixed times. It has worked this way for more than twenty years. The company is Zara.
script.sees: VO: A clothing shop before opening: a manager walking the rails, a handheld scanner, a rail with a gap where the middle sizes were. Cut to a truck on a motorway at dusk. Cut to cartons on a conveyor.
script.title: Cold open: Wednesday, ten to three

script.say:
Most businesses order the way they always have. Once a season, on a feeling, in a large lot.
Zara orders twice a week, on a fixed clock, in small lots, based on what sold.
That one habit helped a shop in a small Spanish city become one of the largest clothing businesses in the world. Today I want to show you how that habit works, and how a trader or distributor with forty people can run the same rhythm on a sheet.
This is Built to Run. Stories of businesses that run on systems, not on memory.
script.sees: FULL: Palak at her desk, window light.
script.title: The question

script.say:
Let me start with a problem you already know.
Every season, you place a bet. Before Diwali. Before the wedding season. Before summer. You commit money to stock months before a single customer walks in.
Some of that stock flies. You run out by the second week, and the customer goes next door. Some of it does not move at all. It sits in the godown. By March it is on a discount table, or it is still sitting there.
Then the season itself becomes a chase. Which branch needs what. What came in. What is stuck. Why the count in the godown does not match the book. And all of those questions come to one desk. Yours.
The bet has a price that never shows up as one line in the accounts. It is the money sitting in cartons instead of in the bank. It is the interest on the limit you drew to buy them. It is the discount you give in March to get some of that money back. And it is the sale you lost in October, when the thing the customer wanted was not on the shelf.
Most owners accept this as the nature of trade. Zara treated it as a design problem.
script.sees: FULL: Palak to camera. Cutaways to [BR-05] and [BR-06] in the third and fourth paragraphs.
script.title: Act 1: The bet every trader places

script.say:
Picture a distributor in Indore. Forty people. Two godowns and a counter.
The order to the company goes in when the owner remembers, or when a salesman shouts that something is finished. The quantity is what was ordered last time, plus a little extra, to be safe.
The counter staff know things the owner does not. They know that three customers asked for a pack size you do not stock. They know a new shade is moving. But that knowledge stays at the counter. It goes home with them at eight.
And when the owner walks in the next morning, he asks the same question he asked yesterday. "Order ho gaya?"
None of this is laziness. Everyone is working hard. The problem is that the order has no fixed day, no fixed rule and no home for what the counter knows. So the owner becomes the memory, the follow-up department and the feedback loop, all at once.
[your own line]
script.sees: PIP: A trader's desk: a diary with order quantities, a calculator, a phone full of messages, cartons stacked behind. Palak bottom right.
script.title: The owner's desk

script.say:
Zara began with exactly that problem.
Amancio Ortega started making clothes in a small workshop in A Coruña, a port city in the north-west of Spain, in 1963. In 1975 he opened the first Zara shop in the same city.
The story the company's admirers tell is that a German buyer cancelled a large order of lingerie. Ortega's money was stuck in unsold goods. So he opened a shop near his factory and sold them himself. That story is repeated in Harvard Business Review. Treat it as the company's own legend, not as an audited fact.
What is on the record is the lesson he seems to have drawn. Stock nobody ordered is the most expensive thing a clothing business can own.
script.sees: VO: Archive stills of A Coruña harbour and old streets; the first Zara shop front; a 1970s sewing workshop.
script.title: Where Zara began

script.say:
Here is how far that shop went.
Inditex, the group that owns Zara, was formed in 1985 and listed on the Madrid stock exchange in 2001.
In 2008 it had 4,264 stores and sales of about 10.4 billion euros. By 2012, 6,009 stores and nearly 16 billion euros. In 2025, about 5,460 stores and nearly 40 billion euros of sales. These figures are from the company's own annual reports.
Notice one thing. After 2019 the number of stores went down, and sales kept going up. Fewer, larger shops. A large online business. And underneath all of it, the same rhythm of ordering, shop by shop, twice a week.
So how does that rhythm work? I am going to show it to you as five plain mechanisms.
script.sees: PIP: GFX-02, a counter climbing through store numbers and sales by year. Palak bottom right.
script.title: How far it went

script.say:
The first mechanism is a fixed clock.
Inditex says it distributes to its stores twice a week, and that every shipment brings new models. Researchers from MIT and UCLA who worked with the company describe the same thing: two central warehouses in Spain shipping directly to every Zara store in the world, twice a week.
The ordering deadlines were fixed too. As reported in Harvard Business Review in 2004, shops in Spain and southern Europe ordered by three in the afternoon on Wednesday, and by six in the evening on Saturday. Shops in the rest of the world ordered by three on Tuesday and six on Friday.
And the deadline was real. A shop that missed Wednesday waited until Saturday.
The exact days and times may have changed since then. The company does not publish them today. But the principle has not changed.
Then the goods move on a schedule too. Inditex says stock reaches European stores about thirty-six hours after the order is received at the distribution centre. Stores in the Americas and Asia, within forty-eight hours.
Why does a fixed clock matter so much?
Because everyone downstream can plan around it. The factory knows when cutting has to finish. The warehouse knows when the trucks leave. The shop knows when new stock will come and when to clear space for it.
Nobody has to call anybody to ask. The clock answers the question.
There is a second effect, and it is easy to miss. A fixed clock makes every order small. If you know another delivery is coming on Saturday, you do not need to over-order on Wednesday. The fear that drives the extra cartons, "what if we run out", is answered by the next order day. The rhythm itself takes the panic out of the quantity.
Now think of your own order to the company, or to your supplier. When does it go? If the answer is "when it is needed", then the answer is really "when someone remembers". A fixed day is the first home you can give that work.
script.sees: FULL: Palak to camera for the first two paragraphs as the act opens; then PIP over GFX-03, a weekly calendar with order deadlines and delivery days marked.
script.title: Act 2, mechanism one: A fixed clock

script.say:
The second mechanism is the one I find most beautiful as a designer. Zara treats the shop as a sensor.
Most companies try to forecast demand from the head office. They look at last year's numbers and make a guess.
Zara listens to the counter instead. Inditex says its design teams build each season's models from market trends and from customer feedback that comes through its stores. More than seven hundred designers work on its collections.
Accounts of the company from the early 2000s describe how that worked in practice. At the head office in Arteixo, near A Coruña, designers sat with the people who handled each region's shops and with the buyers who planned production. Store managers reported what customers asked for and could not find. A colour. A length. A size. That report went to the people deciding the next order and the next design.
There is a quiet rule on the shop floor too. When a key size of an article runs out in a shop, the article comes off display. A shirt rail without medium and large does not sell, so it is better to pull it and wait for the next delivery. That rule makes the state of the stock visible on the floor itself. Anyone walking past can see which article needs sizes.
So there are two signals. What sold, which the till records. And what was asked for and was not there, which only the person at the counter knows.
In most businesses the second signal is lost every evening. At Zara it had a home and a reader.
Think about what that means in a hardware shop, or a paint dealer, or a garment wholesaler in Indore. The till, or the billing software, tells you what sold. It cannot tell you about the customer who asked for a size you did not have and walked out. That sale never enters any book. Only the person at the counter saw it happen. If nobody asks them, and nobody writes it down, the business learns nothing from it.
script.sees: PIP: Shop floor footage: staff folding, a customer asking at the counter, a manager on a handheld. Then GFX-04, an arrow from the shop counter to the design and buying table.
script.title: Mechanism two: The counter is the sensor

script.say:
The third mechanism is small lots, ordered to what sold.
Inditex says it keeps a low stock commitment at the start of each season, so that it can respond to demand during the season. In plain words: it does not bet the whole season on day one. It makes a first, small run. It watches what sells. Then it makes more of what sold, and stops making what did not.
That habit has a cost and a reward. The cost is that some popular items run out. The reward is that articles are almost never discounted during the regular season.
Here is what the research supports. The MIT and UCLA researchers describe Zara's articles as almost never discounted during the regular selling season. They cite a Harvard Business School case from 2003 for that point. You will see sharper percentages quoted online. They cannot be traced to a primary source, so I will not repeat them.
And to be fair, Zara still has a sale. In 2008 its clearance sales brought in more than a billion euros. The system does not abolish the sale. It keeps it to the end of each season.
Now, the order itself. For years, store managers set their own quantities, size by size, and a team at the warehouse reconciled them. The researchers noticed something every owner will recognise. The managers could not see how much stock the warehouse held, and the warehouse team usually lowered what they asked for. The request was honest, but it was not a clean signal of demand.
So, working with Zara's own team, they built a model. It forecast each article's sales in each shop, by size, over the next few days, and shared the available stock across the whole network. In a controlled pilot in 2006, the new process raised sales by three to four percent and kept products on display for longer. Zara then used it for all its products worldwide.
The store manager's knowledge stayed in the loop. The guesswork in the quantity was taken out.
What is a small lot for you? It depends on your supplier and your margin. For one trader it is ten cartons instead of forty. For another it is one week of stock instead of one month. The test is simple. If the item stops selling tomorrow, how long will the last order sit on your shelf? If the answer is three months, the lot was too big.
script.sees: PIP: GFX-05, two bars comparing a season-start commitment with in-season orders. Then factory floor footage, small bundles of cut fabric.
script.title: Mechanism three: Small lots, ordered to what sold

script.say:
The fourth mechanism is about where things are made and where they wait.
If you want to order twice a week, your supply has to be able to answer twice a week. So Zara keeps a large part of its production close to home.
In its 2021 annual report, Inditex said half of the factories making its garments were in Spain, Portugal, Morocco and Turkey. In 2022, forty-nine percent. In its 2025 results, the company describes this as sourcing close to home, within the season.
The company also says something important about which goods are made where. The most fashion-sensitive garments come from these nearby suppliers, or from its own factories in Spain. Longer-lived basics, the things that sell steadily all year, can be made further away, where it is cheaper and slower.
Fast movers close. Slow movers far. That is the whole rule.
Then all of it passes through central logistics in Spain, with the main centre at Arteixo, next to the head office. Goods arrive, are sorted by shop and leave again, to reach Europe in about a day and a half and the rest of the world in about two days.
Notice that this is a trade. Making things close to home costs more per piece. Zara accepts that cost on the goods where speed matters most, because a fast answer to demand saves more than it costs. On the goods where speed does not matter, it buys cheaper and slower.
For a distributor in Indore, the same rule reads differently but works the same way. The item that sells every day belongs at the counter and in the branch. The item that sells once a month belongs in the central godown, counted, waiting to be called.
script.sees: PIP: GFX-07, a map of Spain, Portugal, Morocco and Turkey around Arteixo, with Asia further out. Then warehouse conveyor footage.
script.title: Mechanism four: Fast movers close, slow movers far

script.say:
The fifth mechanism is the one most owners skip. Count honestly, and count often.
An order built on what sold is only as good as your count. If the book says ten and the shelf has four, every decision after that is wrong.
In 2014, Inditex's chief executive, Pablo Isla, told shareholders that about seven hundred of its stores were already using radio tags on garments, and that around five hundred more would be added every year. The tags let staff check an incoming delivery and count a shop's stock far faster and more accurately, and they flag which garments need reordering.
By the end of 2020, Inditex said those tags, and a single stock record shared by its stores and its website, were in place across all its brands.
In 2019, Isla put the thinking in one line. "Our business model has always been based on very low inventory."
Why does a count drift in the first place? Not because people are dishonest. Because goods move in ways the book does not see. A carton is returned and put on the wrong shelf. A sample is given away. A wrong code is billed. Each small slip is harmless. Over a season they add up to a book nobody trusts, and an owner who walks into the godown to check for himself.
You do not need radio tags. You need a count you trust, done on a fixed day, by a named person, with the difference written down.
script.sees: PIP: Close-up of a garment tag, a handheld reader passing over a rail, a stock count on a screen. Palak bottom right.
script.title: Mechanism five: Count honestly, and often

script.say:
Let me put the five mechanisms through the questions this series always asks.
Where does the work live? In a fixed order cycle and a shared record of each shop's stock, not in one person's head.
How can anyone see the state of the work? The deadline is visible. The truck either came or it did not. The rail with missing sizes shows it on the floor.
What is the feedback loop? The counter reports, twice a week, to the people who decide what to make.
How are errors caught? By a model that checks the request against what actually sold, and by a count that does not depend on memory.
And what happens when the owner is away? Amancio Ortega stepped down as chairman in 2011. In 2011 the group sold about 13.8 billion euros. In 2025, nearly 40 billion. The orders went in twice a week, whoever sat in the chair.
script.sees: PIP: GFX-08, the six questions on one card, each ticked with a short Zara answer.
script.title: What happens when the owner is away

script.say:
Every system looks good in a good year. So let us look at the bad years.
The first test was Spain itself. After 2008, Spain went into a deep recession. By the start of 2013, about twenty-seven percent of Spanish workers were unemployed. That is from Spain's own statistics office.
Zara's home market was in trouble. And yet, between 2008 and 2012, Inditex grew its sales from about 10.4 billion euros to nearly 16 billion. It went from 4,264 stores to 6,009.
Spain's share of its store sales fell from twenty-five percent to twenty-one percent in a single year. So growth came from abroad, while the home market shrank as a share.
I want to be careful here. A twice-weekly order does not create growth on its own. But it meant each shop was stocked to what its own customers bought, in a year when Spanish customers were buying less. A shop that orders what sold does not drown in a recession. It simply orders less.
Every owner watching this has lived through a slow year. A market that goes quiet for six months. A big customer who stops paying. In a slow year, the business that ordered big in advance is stuck with the stock and the loan behind it. The business that orders every few days feels the slowdown in its next order, not in its godown. It loses sales, like everyone else. It does not also lose its cash.
script.sees: FULL: Palak to camera for the opening line as the act opens; then PIP over archive footage of Spanish streets in 2012 and GFX-09, a line chart of Inditex sales against Spanish unemployment.
script.title: Act 3: The test. A country in recession

script.say:
The second test was harder. In the first three months of the 2020 financial year, up to eighty-eight percent of Inditex's stores were closed at some point.
Sales in that quarter fell forty-four percent. The group reported a loss of 409 million euros. Much of that loss came from a one-off provision for a plan to close or absorb between one thousand and twelve hundred smaller stores.
Look at the stock. At the end of April 2020, inventory was ten percent lower than a year before. That is what you would expect when shops order what sold. When selling stopped, ordering slowed with it.
And the stores became small warehouses. Staff packed online orders from their own stockrooms. That depends on knowing exactly what is in each stockroom, and that is what the tags and the single stock record across stores and website gave them.
For the full year 2020, sales fell twenty-eight percent to about 20.4 billion euros. Profit fell seventy percent. But online sales grew seventy-seven percent. The company says the single stock record alone added 1.2 billion euros of online sales, and that its supply chain kept running normally because so much of it was close to home.
Days of stock rose to about ninety-four that year. By 2025 they were back to about seventy-one.
What does this test tell us? Not that the system made Zara immune. It did not. The company lost money in a quarter for the first time as a listed business. But the system bent instead of breaking. The order cycle shrank when sales shrank. The stock was in one record, so it could be sold through a different door. And, by the company's own account, the supply close to home kept moving. A business that runs on a rhythm can slow the rhythm down. A business that runs on one big bet has already placed it.
script.sees: PIP: Archive news footage of shuttered high streets in 2020, then a stockroom with staff packing online orders. GFX-10 shows the 2020 figures one by one.
script.title: The pandemic

script.say:
There is a third test, and it is not about stock. It is about the people and the planet behind the model. I want to state it as plainly as the record allows.
In 2011, Brazilian labour authorities found workers in degrading conditions at workshops in São Paulo making Zara garments through an outsourced supplier. Zara said that outsourcing was unauthorised and in breach of its code of conduct.
In 2017, shoppers in Istanbul found notes in Zara garments from workers at a supplier's factory that had closed owing them wages. Inditex said it had met its contractual obligations and was working with other brands on a hardship fund for the workers.
And there is the wider argument about fast fashion. Global clothing production roughly doubled between 2000 and 2015, according to the Ellen MacArthur Foundation. Critics argue that a model built on frequent new styles makes people buy more and wear each piece less.
I am not here to settle that debate. I am here to look at one narrow thing: how a business decides what to order, and when. That part is worth learning from. The rest is worth knowing, so that we learn the right thing.
script.sees: PIP: Slow footage of a garment factory, workers from behind or hands only. Then a landfill of textiles, wide and still.
script.title: The honest limits

script.say:
Now let me speak to you directly, as the owner of a business with fifteen or a hundred people.
You are not Inditex. You do not have two warehouses in Spain, seven hundred designers, or researchers from MIT writing models for you. Nobody is asking you to.
But every mechanism we just saw started as a habit before it became software. A fixed day. A small order. A report from the counter. An honest count. Those are habits any shop or distributor can run on a sheet.
Here are four. Each one comes from a moment in the story you have just seen.
And one more thing before we start. Do not try all four in the same week. Start with one process. The order to your main supplier, or the stock of your twenty fastest items. Run it for a month. Then add the next.
script.sees: FULL: Palak to camera for the whole act. Lesson titles appear as lower-third text.
script.title: Act 4: What this means for a business of forty people

script.say:
Remember the Zara manager watching the clock at ten to three on Wednesday.
Choose your order days. Two a week is a good start. Tuesday and Friday, for example. Write them down. Tell your supplier, your godown and your branches.
Then agree the delivery day that follows each order. And keep both, even in a busy week. Especially in a busy week.
What changes is that nobody has to ask "has the order gone?" The day answers it. If an order is late, everyone can see it is late, because the day has passed.
For a trader, that is the order to the company. For a manufacturer, it is the raw material order. For a firm like ours, it is the day the week's work is handed out.
If your supplier cannot deliver on a fixed day today, start with your own side. Fix the day you send the order. The supplier usually follows a customer who is predictable.
script.sees: FULL: Cut briefly to [Z2], a wall calendar with Tuesday and Friday circled.
script.title: Lesson one: Fix the order day and the delivery day, and keep them

script.say:
Remember the first small run, and the second order based on what actually sold.
On your order day, the order is simple. Look at what sold since the last order. Look at what is on the shelf. Order to refill what sold, not what you hope will sell.
Here is an example, with invented numbers. You sold twelve cartons of an item since Friday. You keep a level of fifteen on the shelf. You have three left. So you order twelve. Not twenty, because the salesman is confident. Not thirty, because a scheme is running. Twelve, because twelve sold.
That means smaller orders, more often. It feels risky at first. You worry about running out. But a business that orders twice a week can correct itself twice a week. A business that orders once a season can correct itself once a season.
And keep Zara's rule about place. Fast movers close: at the counter, in the branch, in the van. Slow movers far: in the central godown, counted, called when needed.
script.sees: FULL: GLIMPSE, 3 seconds: [S1], a masked sheet with columns for item, sold since last order, on shelf, to order. Then [Z3].
script.title: Lesson two: Order what sold, in small lots

script.say:
Remember the store manager reporting what customers asked for and could not find.
Your counter staff hear things every day that you never hear. A pack size. A colour. A brand a customer named. Today that knowledge goes home with them.
Give it a home. One column on a sheet, or one page in a notebook at the counter. "Asked for, not in stock." Date, item, how many times. Two minutes a day.
Then read it on order day. Not once a month. On order day, next to what sold.
The counter becomes the sensor. And the person at the counter learns that what they notice changes what the business buys. That is a quiet kind of respect, and staff feel it.
script.sees: FULL: Cut briefly to [Z1], a counter notebook headed "Asked for, not in stock". Then GLIMPSE, 3 seconds: [S2], the masked dashboard.
script.title: Lesson three: Make the counter the sensor, and give its report a home

script.say:
Remember the tags on every garment, and the single stock record during the pandemic.
You do not need tags. You need a count you trust. Pick your fast movers, maybe twenty items. Count them every week, on a fixed day, by a named person. Write down the difference between the book and the shelf.
The first few weeks, the differences will surprise you. That is not bad news. It is the first honest number you have had.
Do not punish the person who finds the difference. If finding a gap gets someone shouted at, gaps stop being found. Thank them, write the reason next to the number, and fix the cause.
Every order you place after that is built on something true.
script.sees: FULL: Cut briefly to [Z4], a hand with a tally sheet counting cartons on a godown shelf. Then GLIMPSE, 2 seconds: [S3], a masked reminder.
script.title: Lesson four: Count honestly, and often

script.say:
I came to this as a designer. When I joined my family's firm, VSP Consultants, I saw the same problem Zara solved, in a different shape. Our work is files and deadlines, not shirts. But the work had no fixed day and no home. It lived in people's heads, and the follow-ups came to one desk.
So we gave it a rhythm. A day when the week's work is handed out. A day when the score comes back. A place where anyone can see what is done and what is stuck. We run on that every day.
This is the work I do now, through Venture Drafters. I set up that kind of rhythm for owner-led businesses, one process at a time, on your own sheet. We train your team on it, and we keep it running.
Zara did not get there by working harder than everyone else. Its people work hard, but so do yours. It got there by deciding when to order, by listening to the counter, and by keeping to the clock, year after year.
The owner's problem is a design problem. Give the work a day, a home and a reader, and fewer follow-ups come back to your desk.
If you want to see how this looks for your business, book a 30-minute call. The link is in the description.
script.sees: FULL: Palak at her desk. GLIMPSE, 3 seconds: [S2], the masked dashboard, during the second paragraph. [D3] under the last line before the call to action.
script.title: Close: What I do

script.say: Thank you for watching Built to Run.
script.sees: FULL: Palak's last line, then the end card: Venture Drafters logo, tagline "See everything. Chase nothing." Captions on a dark bar.
script.title: End card

snapshot.notes:
Built to Run: Stories, episode 10: Zara. The shop that orders twice a week.. Source: Marketing/case-studies/10-zara.md (script, b-roll list, slide outline, fact sheet, sources, cut-downs). Fortnightly Monday slot 2027-03-15, 11:00.

Do not claim (from the fact sheet):
- "Zara gets a design into stores in two weeks" or "in 15 days" as a fixed fact. Figures range from one week to five weeks across secondary sources. Say "a few weeks".
- "Stores receive deliveries every day." The traceable figure is twice a week.
- "Zara never discounts" or "has no sale". Clearance sales exceeded a billion euros in 2008.
- The 15 to 20 percent markdown figure against 30 to 40 percent for European peers, and the "under 10 percent unsold stock against 17 to 20 percent" figure, in any form. Neither could be traced to a primary source (checked 30 October 2026).
- "Managers asked for more than they expected to sell when stock was short." An inference, not stated in the sources seen. The sources say only that managers could not see warehouse stock and that the warehouse team usually lowered requests.
- "Inditex and other brands agreed to compensate the Bravo Tekstil workers." Sources seen show a proposed hardship fund and no full settlement by late 2017.
- Any proximity-factory share after 2022, or a 2019 figure. Not verified against Inditex reports.
- "Zara commits only 15 to 25 percent of production before the season." Widely repeated, not traced to an Inditex statement. Inditex says only that commitment is low.
- "Garments never stay more than a few hours in the Arteixo warehouse." Not verified. Use the 36 and 48 hour delivery times from Inditex.
- The "Zorba" naming story and the cancelled German lingerie order as fact. Both are company lore; the second may be told as "the story usually told".
- "Zara spends nothing on advertising." Commonly said; not checked for this episode.
- Any figure about Amancio Ortega's personal wealth. Not relevant and changes daily.
- The order deadlines (Wednesday 3 pm and so on) as today's schedule. They are from 2004 reporting.
- "Inditex is the largest fashion retailer in the world" as a ranking fact. Say "often described as".
- --

linkedin.text:
I spent this week reading about Zara, and the detail that stayed with me was a clock.

In 2004, Harvard Business Review described the ordering deadlines in Zara's shops. In Spain and southern Europe, three in the afternoon on Wednesday and six in the evening on Saturday. A shop that missed Wednesday waited until Saturday.

As a designer, I find that more interesting than any technology the company bought later. A fixed clock is a design decision. It tells the factory when to cut, the warehouse when to load and the shop when to clear space. Nobody has to ask whether the order went. The day answers.

Most owners I meet place their main order when someone remembers. The quantity is last time's, plus a little extra. Then they spend the week asking whether it went.

The smallest change I know is to give that order two fixed days a week, and keep them.

If you run a trading or distribution business, which day does your main order go today?

There is a sale that never enters any book.

A customer asks for a size, a pack or a colour you do not have. They leave. The till records nothing. The only person who knows is standing at the counter, and that knowledge goes home with them in the evening.

Zara treated that person as its most important sensor. Inditex says its collections draw on customer feedback that comes through its stores, and its store managers' reports reach the people deciding the next order and the next design.

In my family's firm the counter is a client call, not a shop. The pattern is the same. The person closest to the customer hears the problem first. If there is no place to write it down, the business learns about it last, usually through the owner.

Giving that report a home is not a software project. It is one page and one habit: read it on order day, next to what sold.

In 2020, Inditex, the group that owns Zara, reported its first quarterly loss as a listed company. I think the way it lost money is worth studying.

In the first quarter, up to 88 percent of its stores were closed at some point. Sales fell 44 percent. But inventory at the end of April was 10 percent lower than a year earlier. When selling stopped, ordering slowed with it, which is what you would expect when shops order what sold.

Over the full year, online sales grew 77 percent. Inditex said a single stock record across stores and online added 1.2 billion euros of online sales. Stores packed web orders from their own stockrooms.

The lesson I take is not about scale. It is that a business running on a rhythm can slow the rhythm down. A business that placed one big bet in advance has already placed it.

Most owners have lived through a slow year. The question is whether the slowdown shows up in your next order, or in your godown.

---
