tags: asian paints. which shade, in which town, on which day.

script.say:
A paint shop in a small town. Four o'clock in the afternoon. A woman has brought a shade card from home. Her finger is on one small square of colour. A soft green, the colour she wants for her daughter's room.
The shopkeeper does not go to the back. He does not phone the depot. He types a number into a machine on his counter. The machine pumps a few drops of this, a few drops of that, into a can of white paint. The can goes onto a shaker. A few minutes later she walks out with her green.
That shop does not stock her green. It never did. It stocks a few cans of base and a rack of colours. Everything else is made at the counter.
script.sees: VO: Reconstruction, filmed with a local dealer's permission. A small-town paint shop at four in the afternoon. A customer's finger rests on one chip in a shade card. The shopkeeper types a code. A machine on the counter whirs and drips colour into a white can. The can goes onto a shaker.
script.title: Cold open: the counter

script.say:
Asian Paints shows two thousand two hundred shades on its current fan deck. No shop in India can keep two thousand two hundred shades, in four pack sizes, in every range.
So how does a paint company decide which colour to keep in which town, on which day? That is the question for this episode. The answer is not a bigger warehouse. It is a design decision, taken decades ago, and a habit of planning that most companies in India did not have.
This is Built to Run. Stories of businesses that run on systems, not on memory.
script.sees: FULL: Palak at her desk, a shade card open in her hand.
script.title: The question

script.say:
Before we go to Asian Paints, let us start at your counter.
A customer calls. He wants a size you do not have. Or a finish. Or a grade. Or a colour. You have two choices, and both are bad. You say "not in stock", and he buys from the shop down the road. Or you start keeping everything, just in case. Then your godown fills with stock that does not move, and your money sits on the shelf.
Most owners I meet handle this from memory. Their own, or a trusted manager's. The manager knows that this item sells before Diwali. That one sells in the rains. This customer always wants the heavy gauge. When a dealer phones and asks, "Stock hai?", the answer comes from someone's head.
That works while the business is small enough to fit in one head. It stops working when the range grows, or the manager goes on leave, or you open a second godown. Then you find out last. The customer finds out first.
script.sees: FULL: Palak to camera.
script.title: Act 1: your own counter

script.say:
Now take that problem and multiply it.
Paint comes in many ranges, from cheap distemper to premium emulsion. Each range comes in several pack sizes. Each one, in principle, comes in every shade on the card. And it is sold in tens of thousands of small shops, from metros to towns that are not on most maps.
Demand is not even. It rises before festivals. It falls in the rains. It is different in Tamil Nadu and in Punjab. A company that tried to stock every shade, in every size, in every town, would drown in paint. A company that stocked too little would lose the sale to the shop next door.
Every new shade on the card makes the problem worse. More choice for the customer means more ways for the shop to be wrong.
Asian Paints has been the largest paint company in India since 1967. It got there by solving this problem earlier, and more carefully, than anyone else in the trade. To see how, we have to go back to a garage.
script.sees: PIP: GFX-04 builds on screen: one shade card, then four pack sizes, then several product ranges, then a map of India filling with dots.
script.title: The size of the paint problem

script.say:
1942. Bombay. The war has cut paint imports. Four friends rent a garage and start making paint. Their names are Champaklal Choksey, Chimanlal Choksi, Suryakant Dani and Arvind Vakil. The company's historian, Anupam Gupta, records a fifth early partner who put in money and later sold out. So the story of four friends is true, but it is not the whole cast.
They are young. They know how to sell paint better than how to make it. And the big market is closed to them. The foreign paint companies sell through a few large distributors in the cities, and those distributors decide which brands reach the shops.
script.sees: VO: Archive footage of 1940s Bombay streets and docks. GFX-01 timeline begins: 1942.
script.title: A garage in wartime Bombay

script.say:
So Asian Paints goes around the door. It sells directly to the shopkeeper, from its own depots. Accounts of the company's history say the first dealer was in Sangli, not in Bombay. Any shop that can pay on time can buy. By 1967 it is the largest paint maker in the country.
Here is the part most retellings skip. A wholesaler does two quiet jobs. He holds stock between the factory and the shop. And he guesses, from memory, what each shop will want next month.
For the shopkeeper, the new arrangement was attractive. He bought from the maker, not from a middleman. But for the company, it carried a hidden cost.
When Asian Paints cut out the wholesaler, it cut out the person doing the guessing. Now there was nobody between the depot and thousands of small shops. If a depot ran out of a fast-selling product before a festival, the company heard about it from an angry dealer.
So it had to know, itself, what each depot would need. Not roughly. Item by item. That is a planning problem. And in India, in the 1960s, almost nobody was solving planning problems with data.
script.sees: PIP: GFX-02: two chains side by side. Left: factory, distributor, wholesaler, shop. Right: factory, company depot, shop.
script.title: The door they went around

script.say:
Let us look at the system Asian Paints built. I will take it in five parts. A machine in an office. A plan for every item at every depot. Trucks that come every day. A machine on the counter. And a calendar.
For each part, I will tell you what is on the record, and what is only a good story. Because this company has attracted a lot of good stories.
script.sees: FULL: Palak to camera.
script.title: Act 2: the system

script.say:
If you read investor blogs, you will find a precise story. In 1970, Asian Paints bought India's first supercomputer. A named model. Eight crore rupees. Before ISRO and before the IITs.
I tried to trace that story to a source. I could not. None of those blogs points to a company document or a record from the time.
Here is what does hold up. Forbes India reported that Asian Paints bought its first mainframe computer in the 1970s, when computers were almost unknown in Indian business, and soon used it to forecast demand. Anupam Gupta, who wrote the company's history, also places the computer in the 1970s, and says it was among the first in India to buy one. He also says Esso and the Tatas bought mainframes in the same period. So "among the first" is fair. "The first" cannot be shown from any record, and I will not say it.
Gupta adds one detail that tells you how serious the decision was. He says the machine cost about a tenth of the company's total assets.
Think about that in your own terms. Imagine spending a tenth of everything your firm owns on a machine whose main job is to tell you what your customers will buy next month. That is not a technology decision. That is a decision about how you want to run the business. Data instead of a wholesaler's memory.
In his account, the point of the machine was to plan ahead. To know what dealers in a region would need, by season and by colour, before the dealers themselves had noticed their shelves were thin.
He also says the computer was used to run a discount for dealers who paid within thirty days. So the same machine that planned the stock also tracked the money. The two were never separate.
script.sees: PIP: Archive stills of a 1970s mainframe room, captioned "A mainframe of the period. Not Asian Paints' machine." Then GFX-06, a claim card with three lines struck through.
script.title: Part one: the computer, and the folklore around it

script.say:
The first question we ask in every story is simple. Where does the work live?
At Asian Paints, the work of deciding what goes where lives in a plan. Not in a sales officer's head.
The company says it has run an integrated planning system since 1999. One system that links the forecast, the factory and the delivery. In 2009 it chose planning software from a company called i2 to forecast about fifteen hundred items and to plan buying, making, moving and stocking across factories, warehouses and depots together. A planner from the company wrote in 2016 about using near real-time information to predict changes in demand within a month.
Today, the company's annual report says its forecasts are made at the depot and item level. It uses historical sales, real-time data, market information and statistical models, including machine learning. The factory plan, the shipping plan and the buying plan all follow from that forecast.
Notice the unit. Not India. Not a region. One item, at one depot.
Compare that with most firms I see. The forecast, if there is one, is a feeling. The owner says, "Last year was good, order a little more." Nobody writes down for which item, or for which customer, or for which godown. At Asian Paints, the feeling was replaced by a number in a cell, and the cell had an address.
That is the real answer to "which colour in which area". The company does not guess for the country and then divide. It builds the forecast from the bottom, item by item, place by place. A spike in one district shows up in that district's numbers. It does not disappear inside a national total.
script.sees: PIP: GFX-05: a grid. Rows are items, columns are depots. Each cell shows a small forecast number. One cell highlights.
script.title: Part two: a plan for every item at every depot

script.say:
A forecast is only useful if the trucks behind it are fast. So, the second question. How can anyone see the state of the work? And the third. Who finds out when something slips?
Look at the network, year by year. In 2013, Forbes India counted about thirty-five thousand dealers. In 2019, the company told investors it had more than sixty thousand retailers and one hundred and thirty-five depots. In 2021, its head of supply chain described about seventy-five thousand dealers, served directly from eight factories and one hundred and forty-three warehouses.
And here is the number I find most useful. In larger towns, a dealer who orders in the morning gets the paint the same day. In the largest cities, a dealer can get two deliveries a day.
Think about what that does to the shopkeeper. He does not need to guess a month ahead. He orders what sold this morning, and it comes this evening. The guessing moves up the chain, to the depot, where it can be done with data.
In that same 2019 presentation, the company said its depots were serving more customers while its finished-goods stock had come down. More shops, less stock. That is what a short cycle buys you.
Money moves on the same short cycle. In 2019 the company said seventy percent of its sales were on three-day payment.
And the state of the work is visible. The company tracks its order fill rate. That means how much of each dealer order was supplied in full. A depot that keeps missing items shows up in that number. Nobody has to phone the head office to complain. The number complains for them.
So when a forecast is wrong, the company finds out within days. Not at the end of the quarter. Not from the owner walking the market.
script.sees: PIP: Footage of trucks loading at a warehouse at dawn, then on a highway. GFX-03: a map with the 2021 network figures counting up.
script.title: Part three: trucks that come every day

script.say:
Now the part that answers the question I started with. How do they choose which shade to keep in which town?
For most shades, they do not choose. They do not keep them at all.
Asian Paints introduced computerised colour matching in the mid-1970s. By 2019 it had more than forty-six thousand ColourWorld outlets. That is its own tinting system, placed in dealers' shops. It was adding about four thousand a year.
Here is how a tinting machine works. The shop keeps a few base paints. Think of them, for illustration, as a white, a mid-tone and a deep base. And it keeps a rack of concentrated colours. Systems like this usually run on two to four bases and about a dozen colourants. Every shade on the card has a recipe stored in the machine. Which base. How many drops of each colour. The machine measures them exactly, pumps them into the base can, and the shaker mixes it. A set like this can make more than a thousand shades.
The supply-chain word for this is postponement. In plain words: keep the common part in stock, and make the special part at the last moment, after the customer has chosen.
Look at what that does to the planning problem. The question used to be: which of two thousand two hundred shades should this shop keep? Now the question is: how many cans of each base, and how many bottles of each colour? That is a short list. It can be forecast. And a wrong guess about a shade costs nothing, because the shade was never made.
This is the fourth question. How are errors caught before they reach the customer? The better answer is a design that removes the error. The most expensive mistake in this trade is the wrong shade, made in bulk, sitting in the wrong town. With tinting at the counter, that mistake cannot happen.
The company keeps refining the rest. In 2023-24 it said a new inventory tool cut its stock norms by about five percent, while service improved. It is also building regional centres for slow-moving items, so the uncertain tail of the range is held once, centrally, not at every depot.
One thing I want to be careful about. You may read that the tinting machines send their data back to head office to drive the forecast. It is plausible. I could not find a public source that says so. So I am not saying it.
script.sees: PIP: Close shots of a tinting machine dispensing into a base can. Then GFX-04 resolves: 2,200 shades on the left, three bases and a dozen colourants on the right, lines connecting them.
script.title: Part four: the machine on the counter

script.say:
The last part is the calendar.
Paint demand follows festivals, and India's festivals do not fall on the same day everywhere. The company's head of supply chain explained it in 2021. Diwali, in October and November, drives demand in the North and the West. Harvest festivals, in February and March, drive it in other regions.
Rain works the other way. Nobody paints an outside wall in a downpour. In the July to September quarter of 2024, the company reported a small fall in volumes and named persistent rains and floods as one reason.
So a depot in the North needs more stock in October. A depot in the South may need it in February. A depot in a flood-hit district needs less in August. One national plan could never get all three right.
There is a lovely story from the company's history, told in Gupta's book and retold by The Ken. Sales of small cans spiked around Trichy every winter. Someone went to find out why. Farmers were painting the horns of their cattle for Pongal. I tell it as company lore, not as a documented case. But it shows exactly why the forecast is built depot by depot. A national total would never have shown you cattle horns in Trichy.
script.sees: PIP: GFX-07: a year strip with festival bands by region and a monsoon band. Then footage of Diwali lights, monsoon rain, cattle at Pongal.
script.title: Part five: the calendar

script.say:
The fifth question in this series is the hardest for any founder. What happens when the owner is away?
At Asian Paints, the founders were not there forever. Arvind Vakil died early. Champaklal Choksey led the company for fifty-five years and died in 1997. By 1999 the company was running its integrated planning system.
I want to be honest. No source I found says the founder's death led to the planning system. The dates sit close together, and that is all. What the record does show is this. The company kept its lead after the founding generation. Paint kept reaching the right depot. That only happens when the knowledge of what sells where has been moved out of one person's head and into a plan that anyone can read.
script.sees: PIP: GFX-01 timeline: 1997, then 1999.
script.title: When the owner is away

script.say:
So, five answers. The work lives in a forecast, one item at one depot. The state of the work shows in the order fill rate. The feedback loop is a daily order and a same-day truck. Errors are prevented by making the shade at the counter. And the plan kept running after the founder.
Now the sixth question. What happened when it broke?
script.sees: PIP: GFX-11: the six questions card, five lines filling in.
script.title: The five answers

script.say:
Every system looks good in a normal year. The question is what it does in a bad one. A founder on leave. A big order that goes wrong. A new rival. A year when nothing sells.
For Asian Paints, the clearest test on the public record is the spring of 2020. I chose it because the company's own people have described, on the record, what they did.
script.sees: FULL: Palak to camera.
script.title: Act 3: the test

script.say:
March 2020. India locks down. Shops close. Many painters leave the cities.
The company's chief executive later described April as completely washed out. For April to June 2020, the company's revenue fell by about forty-three percent compared with the year before.
Then the problems get specific. Some dealers are allowed to open. But the company warehouses that normally serve them sit inside containment zones. The trucks cannot leave.
script.sees: VO: Empty city streets, shuttered shop fronts, a closed paint shop shutter.
script.title: April 2020

script.say:
So the company does something it would never plan in a normal year. It supplies those dealers directly from its factories. A dealer who normally takes small orders now receives up to half a truckload at a time. Paint that reaches an open shop is better than paint stuck behind a closed warehouse door.
That decision tells you something. You can only route around a closed warehouse if you know, item by item, what each shop needs and what each warehouse was holding. A company running on memory would not know where to send the paint.
It also has to keep its own factories running while keeping its workers safe. That is not a small thing in 2020.
At the same time, it uses what it has. Its head of supply chain described how the company began making hand sanitiser from raw materials it already held, and then a painting service with sanitising, so painters could enter homes safely.
script.sees: PIP: Factory gate, a truck pulling out. GFX-02 redraws: the depot box greys out and a direct line runs from factory to shop.
script.title: The workaround

script.say:
Demand came back sooner than many expected. It came back first in smaller towns. People were at home, looking at their own walls.
From July to September 2020, the company's decorative volumes grew eleven percent. From October to December, they grew thirty-three percent.
Here is the moment I find most telling. On the results call, an analyst asked whether those numbers were inflated by pushing stock onto dealers before a price rise. That is an old trick. Fill the channel, and the quarter looks good.
The chief executive said there was "no inventory in the network" that had gone up. He said the company had not pushed stock onto retailers, and believed what it sold had been sold on to customers.
You can only answer that question with confidence if you can see the stock in the channel. That is what a planning system gives you. Not luck. A straight answer.
script.sees: PIP: GFX-08: three bars. April to June: revenue down about 43 percent. July to September: volume up 11 percent. October to December: volume up 33 percent.
script.title: The recovery, and a straight answer

script.say:
I do not want to tell this as a story where the system always wins. There is a second test, and it is still running.
In February 2024, the Aditya Birla Group launched a paint business called Birla Opus, with a commitment of ten thousand crore rupees. It described the new plants as adding forty percent to the industry's capacity.
In the October to December quarter of 2024, Asian Paints reported decorative volumes up just 1.6 percent, revenue down 7.8 percent and a lower margin. The company itself named weak demand, customers moving to cheaper products and a weak festive season.
A planning system does not stop a competitor. It does not make customers spend. What it does is show you the damage early, in detail, depot by depot. What you do about it is still a management decision.
script.sees: PIP: Press-release headlines on screen, then a simple line chart drawn as GFX.
script.title: A second test, still running

script.say:
So here is the sixth answer. When it broke, in 2020, the plan told the company what each shop needed, even when the usual route was closed. When demand returned, the company could say plainly that it had not stuffed its dealers. And when a rival arrived with deep pockets, the numbers showed the pressure quickly, even if they could not make it go away.
Think about your own firm in April 2020. Did you know, that week, what was in each godown, what each customer had on order, and what you could still deliver? Or did you find out by phoning around, one person at a time?
That is what a system is for. Not to prevent bad years. To make sure you see them clearly, and early, and not last.
script.sees: FULL: Palak to camera.
script.title: What the test shows

script.say: You do not run a paint company with seventy-five thousand dealers. You may run a trading firm with forty people and two godowns. Or a factory with three hundred items and fifty regular customers. You do not need a mainframe, or machine learning, or a planning team. But four ideas from this story travel well to your size.
script.sees: FULL: Palak to camera.
script.title: Act 4: what this means for a business of 15 to 100 people

script.say:
Remember the tinting machine. A few bases, many shades.
Look at your own list the same way. Your bases are the items many orders need. The standard sizes. The common grade. The plain carton before printing. The grey fabric before dyeing. The bare frame before the finish. These you must keep in stock, always.
Your shades are the variations. The special finish. The custom print. The rare size one customer asks for twice a year. These you can make or order when the customer confirms. On the quote, you write the lead time, and you stop pretending you keep them.
Start small. Take your top fifty items by sales and mark each one, base or shade. You do not need to sort all three thousand codes in your software on the first day.
When you do this honestly, many owners find their list of "must keep" items is much shorter than their godown suggests. And the question "what should we stock?" becomes a question you can actually answer.
script.sees: FULL: Palak to camera, with a brief PIP insert of [K2], her hand sketching a tree: a few boxes at the root, many leaves.
script.title: Lesson one: split your range into bases and shades

script.say:
Remember the depot-by-item forecast. Asian Paints does not plan India. It plans one item at one depot.
In your firm, that means a row for each item at each place. If you have one godown in Indore and one in Pithampur, the same item gets two rows. If you supply three large customers on a schedule, each one may need its own row for the items they buy.
A total hides the problem. "We have two hundred boxes" means nothing if all two hundred are in the wrong godown. And the customer in Pithampur does not care how many boxes you have in Indore. One row per item per place is the smallest change that makes the problem visible.
script.sees: FULL: Palak to camera, with a brief PIP insert of GFX-05, now with invented item names and two godowns.
script.title: Lesson two: plan each item at each place

script.say:
Remember the morning order and the evening truck. The dealer does not guess a month ahead. He replaces what sold.
At your size, a weekly rhythm is enough. Here is what it looks like on a sheet. One row per item per place. Then these columns. Base or shade. The most you want to hold. What is in stock on Monday morning. What sold last week. What to order this week, which is usually what sold, topped up to your limit. Who places the order. And a column that says done, with a date.
Here is an invented example, to make it concrete. A fastener trader. One row: a standard bolt, at the Indore godown, marked base. The most he wants to hold is four hundred boxes. On Monday there are one hundred and ninety. Last week, two hundred sold. So this week, he orders two hundred. The rare stainless bolt, marked shade, has no stock limit at all. It is ordered only against a confirmed customer order.
On Monday, the sheet is the hand-out. The person whose name is on the row places the order. Nobody waits for the owner to remember.
On Friday, the sheet gives the score. How many times this week did we say "not in stock"? Which items are sitting far above the limit? Those two numbers tell you more about your stock than any long report.
And one rule from the 2020 story. Never push stock onto a customer to make a month look good. If the sheet is honest, you will not need to.
script.sees: FULL: Palak to camera. While she lists the columns, a PIP insert shows GFX-10, a weekly sheet with invented data, columns building one by one, then S1, the sheet scrolling.
script.title: Lesson three: order what sold, every week

script.say:
Remember the cattle horns in Trichy. Somebody noticed a pattern, and the plan took it in.
Every business has its season. A rush before Diwali. A dead month in the rains. A wedding season. A school reopening. A financial year end. In most firms, this lives in one experienced person's memory.
Write it down. Add a column for the month, and keep last year's sales beside this year's. After one year, the sheet remembers what you used to carry in your head. After two, you can see whether this Diwali is better or worse than the last one, item by item. Before a busy month, raise the limit on the items that move. After it, bring it back down. Your senior manager still knows the market better than any sheet. The sheet just means that knowledge stays when he is on leave.
script.sees: FULL: Palak to camera, with a brief PIP insert of GFX-07 redrawn as a twelve-month strip for an invented trading firm.
script.title: Lesson four: write the season down

script.say:
So, which shade, in which town, on which day? Most shades are not kept anywhere. They are made at the counter, in a few minutes, from a few bases. The bases and the fast items are forecast for each depot, one item at a time. Trucks refill the shops every day, and twice a day in the biggest cities. And the calendar, by region, is written into the plan.
Asian Paints chose data over a wholesaler's memory long before it was easy. Then it went further, and removed most of the guessing at the root, by making the shade at the counter.
None of this is clever. It is patient. A company that chose, more than fifty years ago, to put what it knew about its customers into a place anyone could read, and kept doing it.
This is the work I do now. I designed my family's firm's system first, at VSP Consultants in Indore, and we run on it every day. In my family's firm, [your own line]. Now I help owners of firms with fifteen to one hundred people do the same, one process at a time, on their own sheet. For a trader or a manufacturer, a sensible first process is this one: what to keep, what to order, and who orders it on Monday.
If you want to see how this looks for your business, book a 30-minute call. The link is in the description.
script.sees: FULL: Palak to camera.
script.title: Close

script.say: Thank you for watching. Next week, another business, and another system that carried it further than one person could.
script.sees: FULL: , then end card. Navy background, ivory type: "Built to Run. Stories." Next episode title. Booking link.
script.title: End card

snapshot.notes:
Built to Run: Stories, episode 02: Asian Paints. Which shade, in which town, on which day.. Source: Marketing/case-studies/02-asian-paints.md (script, b-roll list, slide outline, fact sheet, sources, cut-downs). Fortnightly Monday slot 2026-11-23, 11:00.

Do not claim (from the fact sheet):
- "In 1970 Asian Paints bought India's first supercomputer", "a CDC 6600", "for Rs 8 crore", "before ISRO and the IITs". Blog folklore with no primary source. The Ken's CDC 6600 image is a stock illustration, not the company's machine.
- "The first Indian private-sector company to use a mainframe for demand forecasting." Not supported. Say "among the first", attributed.
- That an IBM machine was installed in 1970. Single marketing-style source.
- "Trucks refill dealers four times a day" or "1.6 lakh deliveries a day". Stated in an author interview, contradicts the company's own two-a-day figure.
- That tinting-machine dispense data feeds the company's forecasts. No primary source.
- Dealer-level stock norms. Not published.
- Specific market-share figures in the 2024 to 2025 contest (for example "59 to 52 percent"). These come from brokers and vary widely.
- That the founder's death in 1997 caused the 1999 planning system. Dates only.
- Any Asian Paints-specific number of bases or colourants in its tinting system.
- That trucks ran half empty in 2020. The source says dealers received up to half a truckload instead of their usual orders.
- --

4. **They went around the distributors**
   - Foreign firms sold through a few large distributors.
   - Asian Paints sold direct to dealers from its own depots.
   - Largest paint maker in India by 1967.
   - Visual: GFX-02, the two chains.

5. **No wholesaler meant no one to guess**
   - A wholesaler holds stock and guesses next month's demand.
   - Removing him moved both jobs onto the company.
   - It had to forecast each depot itself.
   - Visual: GFX-02 with the wholesaler box fading out.

6. **The computer: fact and folklore**
   - On record: a mainframe in the 1970s, among the first in India, used for forecasting.
   - Not traceable: "1970", "India's first", "Rs 8 crore", "supercomputer".
   - Visual: GFX-06 claim card.

7. **One item, one depot**
   - Integrated planning since 1999.
   - Forecasts made at the depot and SKU level, with statistical and machine-learning models (Annual Report 2023-24).
   - Visual: GFX-05 grid, one cell lit.

8. **Morning order, evening delivery**
   - About 75,000 dealers, 8 factories, 143 warehouses (2021).
   - Same-day delivery in larger towns; two a day in the largest cities.
   - Visual: GFX-03 map with counts.

9. **The state of the work is a number**
   - Order fill rate is tracked for every dealer order.
   - 70 percent of sales on three-day payment (2019).
   - Visual: a single gauge in yellow on navy.

10. **The machine on the counter**
    - A few bases plus about a dozen colourants make over a thousand shades.
    - 46,000+ ColourWorld tinting outlets (2019).
    - Keep the common part; make the special part last.
    - Visual: GFX-04, resolved state.

11. **The calendar, by region**
    - Diwali drives demand in the North and West; harvest festivals elsewhere.
    - Persistent rains cut demand in the July to September quarter of 2024.
    - Visual: GFX-07 year strip.

12. **Less stock, better service**
    - New inventory optimiser: about 5 percent lower inventory norms (FY 2023-24).
    - Regional centres for slow movers.
    - Visual: GFX-09 single number.

13. **The test: April 2020**
    - April to June revenue down about 43 percent.
    - Warehouses in containment zones; dealers supplied straight from factories.
    - Volume up 11 percent, then 33 percent, as demand returned.
    - Visual: GFX-08 three bars.

14. **A second test, still running**
    - A new rival in 2024 with a Rs 10,000 crore commitment.
    - Volumes up 1.6 percent, revenue down 7.8 percent (Oct to Dec 2024).
    - A system shows the damage early. It does not prevent it.
    - Visual: two press-release headlines, side by side.

15. **Lesson: bases and shades**
    - Bases: what many orders need. Always in stock.
    - Shades: variations. Made or ordered on confirmation.
    - Start with your top fifty items.
    - Visual: K2 sketch of the tree.

16. **Lesson: one row per item per place**
    - A total hides the problem.
    - Two godowns means two rows for the same item.
    - Visual: GFX-05 with invented items.

17. **Lesson: order what sold, every week**
    - Monday: the sheet is the hand-out. Named person orders.
    - Friday: count every "not in stock" and every item far over its limit.
    - Write the season down, month by month.
    - Visual: GFX-10 weekly sheet.

18. **Run the business. Not the follow-ups.**
    - Start with one process: what to keep, what to order, who orders it.
    - Book a 30-minute call. The link is in the description.
    - Visual: navy end card, booking link in ivory.

---

script.say:
It is a little after six in the morning, in a village in Anand district, in Gujarat. A woman walks to a small room at the end of the lane. She carries a steel can. There are four people ahead of her. Nobody pushes.
At the window, the secretary pours her milk into a measure. The weight shows on a small screen. A little milk goes into a machine. Within a minute, a slip prints. It shows the date, the shift, her member number, the litres, the fat, the rate and the amount.
She reads it. She folds it. She goes home.
Nobody argued. Nobody phoned anyone. Nobody senior was in the room. This evening she will come back and do it again. So will about 36 lakh other farmers, in about 18,600 villages across Gujarat.
This scene is a composite. I have put it together from the dairy board's own handbook for collection staff. But some version of it happens twice a day, every day.
script.sees: VO: Dawn in a Gujarat village. A woman walks down a lane with a steel can. A small room with a counter window, a short queue. Milk poured, a sample drawn, a slip printing, the slip folded into a pocket. Lower-third caption: "A composite scene, drawn from NDDB's procurement handbook."
script.title: Six in the morning, a village in Anand district

script.say:
I wanted to understand that room. Because it does something most of our businesses cannot do. It settles a payment, fairly, with lakhs of people, every day, without the owner standing there.
So the question for this episode is simple. How does a business owned by lakhs of small farmers pay every one of them correctly, on a day they know, without anyone having to remember, argue or chase?
This is Built to Run. Stories of businesses that run on systems, not on memory.
script.sees: FULL: Palak at her desk, a steel milk can and a folded slip beside her laptop.
script.title: The question

script.say:
Let me start with a desk I know.
A supplier calls at ten. He wants to know when his payment will come. You are not sure. Accounts knows, or thinks it knows. You call accounts. Accounts calls you back at twelve.
At two, a worker says the rate on his slip is wrong. He may be right. He may not be. Either way, it comes to you, because you are the only person both sides will believe.
At five, a customer says the last lot was short. Was it checked before it left? Somebody says yes. Nobody can show it.
None of this is a big problem. Each one takes five minutes. But each one needs you. By the evening, you have been the accounts desk, the quality check and the referee. Everything has come through you.
I saw this in my family's firm, VSP Consultants, before we changed how the work was held. The owner is not slow. The owner is simply the only place where the answer lives.
Now let me take you somewhere the same three questions come up lakhs of times a day. And almost none of them reach the top.
script.sees: FULL: Palak to camera. Cutaways to the desk: sticky notes, a diary, a phone face down.
script.title: Your desk, this morning

script.say:
Go back to Kaira district, in central Gujarat, in the 1940s.
The farmers here kept buffaloes. Their milk went to Bombay under a government milk scheme. The scheme bought from a private dairy at Anand called Polson, which held the right to collect milk across the district. Between Polson and the villages stood the milk contractors.
The union's own history puts it plainly. Nobody had fixed the price paid to the farmer. The contractor fixed it. The farmer sold at that price, or did not sell at all.
That is the position of every small supplier with one buyer. The price is a favour. So is the payment day.
The farmers went to Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel. He gave them specific advice. Form your own cooperative. Own your own processing. Ask the government to buy from you. If it refuses, stop selling to the middlemen, and accept the loss for a while.
On the fourth of January 1946, at a meeting in Samarkha village, the farmers resolved to do exactly that. The government refused. So the farmers stopped selling milk, for fifteen days. Bombay's milk scheme nearly collapsed. The Milk Commissioner came to Anand and accepted their demand.
On the fourteenth of December 1946, the Kaira District Cooperative Milk Producers' Union was registered. Its chairman was Tribhuvandas Patel, a Gandhian and a freedom fighter from Anand.
script.sees: PIP: Archive photographs of Anand and Kaira district in the 1940s. GFX-01, the map of Gujarat with Kheda and Anand marked. Portraits of Sardar Patel and Tribhuvandas Patel as they are named.
script.title: Kaira, 1946: a price set by someone else

script.say:
The strike won the farmers a buyer. It did not yet solve the harder problem.
Think about the transaction itself. A farmer with two buffaloes brings a few litres. Someone has to measure it, judge its quality, write it down, and pay for it, on some day.
At every one of those steps, a person with more power can cheat a person with less. A thumb on the scale. A low reading. A missing entry. A payment that comes late, or not at all. Under the contractors, each step depended on trusting one man.
Tribhuvandas Patel insisted on two rules from the start. Every village society was open to every milk producer, regardless of caste, creed or community. And every member had one vote, whatever his wealth. The union's own account records both.
Those rules settled who belonged. The next question was harder. How could a small room in each village treat everyone the same, twice a day, with nobody from Anand watching?
In May 1949, a young engineer arrived in Anand to serve out a government bond at the creamery. His name was Verghese Kurien. In his autobiography, I Too Had a Dream, he called the town "excruciatingly unexciting and conservative." He meant to leave as soon as he could. Tribhuvandas Patel asked him to stay a little and help set up the union's equipment.
He stayed for the rest of his working life. But notice the order. The farmers built the union first.
script.sees: PIP: GFX-03: one farmer, one contractor, four questions between them: weight, quality, record, payment day. Then a portrait of Verghese Kurien and the cover of his autobiography.
script.title: The real problem was trust

script.say:
Here is what I noticed when I read the handbook that India's National Dairy Development Board gives to milk procurement staff. It describes the village counter in plain steps. There is no slogan in it.
There are five mechanisms. A fixed rhythm. A test done in front of the person. A record the farmer carries home. A payment on a known day. And one rule, the same in every village.
Let me take them one at a time.
script.sees: FULL: Palak to camera, the NDDB handbook open on the desk beside her.
script.title: Five things the counter does

script.say:
The first mechanism is the rhythm.
Every morning and every evening, members bring their milk to the society at set times. The handbook lists collection twice a day as the society's first function. The truck from the union arrives on the society's fixed schedule, picks up the milk, and leaves. If you are late, the milk misses the truck.
This rhythm was not a management idea. Milk forced it. Milk spoils. Buffaloes are milked morning and evening. So the business had to move twice a day, every day, through festivals, and through the days when the secretary has a fever.
But look at what the rhythm does for management. Nobody needs to be reminded to bring milk. Nobody needs to ask the driver when he is coming. Nobody needs to ask whether collection is open today. The time itself is the instruction.
In June 1948, the union was pasteurising about 250 litres a day from two village societies. By the end of that year, 432 farmers had joined, and the union handled 5,000 litres a day. That growth did not need more supervision. It needed more people arriving at the same two times.
In most of our firms, the rhythm is the owner. Dispatch happens when he asks. The review happens when he remembers. Payment happens when someone chases. Take the owner away, and the rhythm stops.
At the village counter, the rhythm belongs to the day, not to a person.
script.sees: PIP: Morning queue at a collection centre, then the same counter in evening light. Cans lifted onto a truck. GFX-04: a clock with two marks, morning and evening, and a truck leaving at a fixed time.
script.title: One: a fixed rhythm, twice a day

script.say:
The second mechanism is the test.
Milk is paid for by its quality, and for most of Amul's history, quality meant fat. A litre with more fat is worth more. So the fat reading is the money.
The old method was called the Gerber test. You put sulphuric acid into a thin glass tube called a butyrometer. You add a measured amount of milk, then a little amyl alcohol. You seal it, shake it, spin it in a centrifuge for five minutes, and read the fat off a scale on the glass. It works. But it is slow, it uses acid, and at a busy counter with a few hundred members, it takes time.
So the dairy board worked with a Danish manufacturer on a small electronic tester for village use. It reads fat from the way light scatters through milk, and shows the number on a display. Today, many societies use an automatic milk collection unit. The weighing scale and the milk analyser are joined to a small computer. The member's number goes in. The machines capture the weight and the fat. The rate comes from a chart the union sends. The slip prints.
In the older counters, the result itself rode on the rhythm. The handbook describes the truck crew bringing back the fat slip of the previous shift, along with the clean cans. The answer arrived on schedule, with the truck, not when someone remembered to send it.
Here is the detail I find most important. The handbook says test results are recorded against a sample number, not a name, so the tester does not know whose milk he is testing. And if a member doubts a reading, she can ask for a retest before the samples are thrown away.
The handbook also notes what happened when electronic testers and collection units arrived. Member participation and trust grew.
Think about why. The test is fair, yes. But more than that, it is seen to be fair, by the person whose money depends on it, at the moment it happens. There is nothing to argue about later, because nothing was decided out of sight.
script.sees: PIP: A sample poured into a small beaker. Close-up of a glass butyrometer and a centrifuge. An electronic milk analyser display. An automatic collection unit at a counter, slip printing.
script.title: Two: the test, in front of the farmer

script.say:
The third mechanism is the record.
Every pour is written in two places. Once in the society's purchase register. And once in the member's own card or passbook, which she keeps. Where the counter is computerised, she also gets the printed slip. Date. Morning or evening. Cow or buffalo. Her member number. Weight. Fat. Rate. Amount.
So the work lives in a place both sides can see. Not in the secretary's memory. Not in a diary in a drawer. On a piece of paper in the farmer's hand, and in a register the auditor will check.
The newer systems go further. A dairy board presentation on collection software describes a digital passbook and a text-message service, so a farmer can check her quantity, her quality, today's price and her balance due, without asking anyone.
This is the first of my six questions. Where does the work live? Here, it lives on the slip and in the passbook.
It also answers the second question. How can anyone see the state of the work? The farmer sees it before she leaves the window. Litres, fat, rate, amount. If something is wrong, she knows in a minute, not at the end of the month.
Compare that with a supplier in your city waiting for his payment. He does not know what you have recorded against his name. He finds out when the money arrives, or does not. So he calls. And the call comes to you.
script.sees: PIP: GFX-05: the anatomy of the slip, each field lit in turn: date, shift, type of milk, member number, litres, fat, rate, amount. Then a handwritten passbook page with invented entries.
script.title: Three: the record the farmer carries home

script.say:
The fourth mechanism is the payment day.
I want to be exact here, because this part is often told loosely. The payment cycle at a village society is not the same everywhere, and it has changed over time.
The dairy board's handbook says a society pays its members daily, weekly or every ten days, as its elected managing committee decides. The same handbook says the union pays each society through the bank at a regular interval, weekly or every ten days. That interval is generally not changed, and it is the same for all societies. A government note in 2016 described the sector's cycles as weekly and ten-day. And in 2021, the managing director of the Kaira union wrote that each society is paid once in ten days.
So the cycle varies. What does not vary is that it is fixed, and known in advance.
The price is fixed in the same way. It is set per kilogram of fat, from the union's chart, not by the secretary. The federation reported paying 337 rupees per kilogram of fat in 2009 to 2010, and 765 rupees in 2019 to 2020. The farmer does not negotiate that number at the window. She checks it.
Since the end of 2016, payments have also moved into farmers' bank accounts.
At the end of the year, there is one more payment. Part of the society's surplus goes back to members as a bonus, in proportion to the milk each one supplied.
That is the third of my six questions. What is the feedback loop? Here, it runs on a timetable. Every shift, the slip. Every cycle, the money. Every month, the committee meets. Every year, the bonus and the audit.
A farmer does not need to ask when she will be paid. A secretary does not need to decide when to pay. A chairman does not need to approve each payment. The calendar decides.
script.sees: PIP: GFX-06: a calendar strip with three versions side by side, labelled daily, weekly and every ten days, each with its payment days marked in yellow.
script.title: Four: payment on a known day

script.say:
The fifth mechanism is the structure, and it is simpler than it sounds.
At the bottom is the village society, owned by its members. In the middle is the district union, owned by the societies. At the top is the state federation, formed by the unions. In Gujarat, that federation is GCMMF, set up in 1973, which sells under the Amul brand. Members elect the leaders at each level. Professional managers answer to those leaders.
Each tier does only what it is placed to do well. The village receives, tests, records and pays. The union buys all of the societies' milk, processes it, and supplies feed, vets and breeding services. The federation sells, under one name.
This answers my fourth question. How are errors caught before they travel? At the society, after each shift, the whole collection is sampled and tested again as one, which the handbook calls the general test. At the union, the milk is tested again at the dock. An auditor checks that every member has a passbook and that every pour is entered.
And since the 1990s, the Kaira union has chilled milk at the society itself, below four degrees within one to two hours of milking, so quality does not slip on the road. By 2016 to 2017, it had a bulk milk cooler in every one of its 1,202 village societies. Its tankers now carry sealed automatic samplers, so each society's sample is drawn by a machine, not a hand.
And it answers my fifth question. What happens when the owner is away? At the village counter, there is no owner. The committee is elected and unpaid. The secretary is paid to run the counter. The rate chart comes from the union. The rule is the same in Anand as in a village two hundred kilometres away. Nobody needs to be present for it to be kept.
script.sees: PIP: GFX-07: the three-tier diagram, with the village society repeated many times along the base, the district union above, the state federation at the top. Then a bulk milk cooler at a society, and a tanker on a highway.
script.title: Five: one rule, the same in every village

script.say:
Notice what the counter does not need.
It does not need the chairman to approve each payment. It does not need a call from Anand to open on time. It does not need the secretary to be a good judge of character, or the farmer to trust him personally. It does not need anyone to remember who brought what last Tuesday.
All of that has been moved out of people's heads, and into the rhythm, the test, the slip and the cycle. What is left for people is the work itself. Pouring, testing, loading, paying.
That is the difference between a system and a set of good people. Good people get tired. They go on leave. They leave. A rhythm does not.
Even the best-known person in this story eventually left, and not happily. I will come to that. The counters did not notice. They opened the next morning, at the same time.
script.sees: PIP: Palak's hand sketching the counter on paper: a box for the window, four arrows out of it labelled rhythm, test, record, day.
script.title: What the counter does not need

script.say:
Every system looks good on a normal Tuesday. The real question is what happens when something breaks. A flood of supply. A collapse in demand. A crisis nobody planned for.
Amul has been tested more than once. I want to show you three tests. The first, in the 1950s, was too much milk. The second, from 1970, was scale, whether the counter could be copied across India. The third was March 2020.
script.sees: FULL: Palak to camera.
script.title: Every system meets a bad year

script.say:
Buffaloes give about two and a half times as much milk in winter as in summer. By 1953, the Bombay scheme could not take the extra winter milk. Farmers were once again selling their surplus to middlemen, at low rates.
This mattered for the whole design. The farmer pours twice a day because the society will take all of her milk. If the society cannot take it in winter, the rhythm breaks, and the contractors come back.
The union's answer was a factory. A plant to turn surplus milk into milk powder and butter, costing about fifty lakh rupees. President Rajendra Prasad laid its foundation stone in November 1954. Prime Minister Nehru opened it on the thirty-first of October 1955. The union describes it as the first plant to make these products from buffalo milk at commercial scale.
The lesson is quiet, but important. When the promise at the counter came under pressure, they did not change the counter. They built capacity behind it, so the promise could hold.
script.sees: PIP: Archive images of the Anand dairy plant in the 1950s. GFX-09: a summer bar and a winter bar two and a half times taller.
script.title: Test one: the winter surplus

script.say:
The second test was scale.
On the thirty-first of October 1964, Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri came to Anand to open the union's cattle feed plant. He spent a night with farmers in the district. Then he asked Kurien to repeat the Anand model across the country. The National Dairy Development Board was set up at Anand in 1965. Operation Flood began in 1970.
What travelled was not a brand. It was the counter. A village society, a district union, a state federation, and the same routine at the bottom. Collect twice a day. Test. Record. Pay.
By the end of the first phase, in 1981, the programme had formed 13,270 village dairy cooperatives, covering about seventeen and a half lakh farm families. By the end of the third phase, the count was 72,744 cooperatives and about 93 lakh families. Those are the dairy board's own figures.
A rule that only works because one good person is watching cannot be copied seventy-two thousand times. A rule that is the same at every counter can.
script.sees: PIP: Archive photograph of Lal Bahadur Shastri. GFX-10: a map of India, milk sheds appearing phase by phase, with two counters: 13,270 societies, then 72,744.
script.title: Test two: copying the counter across India

script.say:
The third test is the one I find most striking.
India's lockdown began on the twenty-fifth of March 2020. For three days, Amul's sales rose as people stocked up. On the fourth day, they fell by about thirty percent. Hotels, sweet shops and restaurants shut. Many smaller and private dairies stopped buying milk.
Think about what that means at the village counter. A farmer still has buffaloes to milk, twice a day. If nobody buys, the milk is lost, and so is the month's income.
Amul did not stop collecting. Its managing director said in April 2020 that it was taking ten to fifteen percent more milk than usual, because the smaller dairies had closed. He said it was still paying forty-two rupees a litre for buffalo milk at six percent fat, and thirty-one rupees for cow milk at three and a half percent fat. The extra milk went into butter and milk powder, which keep for a year or two.
At its annual meeting that July, the federation said the Gujarat unions had procured an additional 35 lakh litres a day during the lockdown, giving about 800 crore rupees extra to rural milk producers. In June, the managing director said Amul had put about 9,000 crore rupees into the rural economy, in Gujarat and the other states where it works.
Why could it do this? Not only because people made brave decisions in a boardroom, though they did. It was because the counter already worked on a rhythm everyone knew. The society takes the milk. The test is done in front of you. The rate comes from the chart. The money comes on the known day. Nothing about that had to be invented in a crisis. It only had to keep going.
script.sees: PIP: Empty Indian streets in the 2020 lockdown. A milk tanker moving on an empty road. Butter blocks and milk powder bags in a store. GFX-11: one line for sales dipping, one for procurement rising.
script.title: Test three: March 2020

script.say: So, my sixth question. What happened when it broke? Demand broke. The counter did not. Morning and evening, the windows opened, the milk was tested, the slips printed, and the payments followed on the cycle.
script.sees: FULL: Palak to camera.
script.title: What the test showed

script.say:
Before I draw lessons, let me be honest about the limits.
Amul is not a forty-person firm. It is a federation of cooperatives, owned by its own suppliers. In its early years, the state bought its milk on contract at stable prices. Operation Flood was funded with donated milk powder and World Bank loans. Its boards are elected, and like many cooperatives in India, it has a political life. Chairmanships have been contested. Kurien himself resigned as chairman of the federation in March 2006, ahead of a no-confidence motion by his own board. Operation Flood also had serious critics, who questioned who gained most from it.
And yet the counters kept opening after 2006, morning and evening, as before.
You cannot copy a federation. You should not try.
But you can copy the counter. Because the counter is the place where your business meets a supplier, a worker or a customer. And that moment either needs you, or it does not.
Here are four things I take from Anand.
script.sees: FULL: Palak to camera.
script.title: Where the comparison stops

script.say:
First. A fixed rhythm removes the need to chase.
The farmer does not ask when collection opens. It opens at the same time every day.
In your firm, pick the one thing you chase most. For many owners, it is dispatch. Give it a time. Dispatch closes at four. Whatever is packed, checked and billed by four goes today. Whatever is not goes tomorrow, and the sheet shows why. Then give the week a rhythm. On Monday, everyone gets their list. On Friday, everyone sees their score.
Once the time is fixed, you stop being the alarm clock. You no longer walk to the floor at six in the evening to ask, "ho gaya?" Four o'clock has already answered.
script.sees: FULL: Palak to camera. Brief cutaway to a dispatch bay with cartons stacked.
script.title: Lesson one: a fixed rhythm removes the need to chase

script.say:
Second. A test done in front of the person removes the argument.
At the counter, the farmer watches her milk being tested. If she doubts it, she asks for a retest, there and then. Nobody argues a week later.
Most disputes in our firms come from a check done out of sight. The customer says the lot was short. The supervisor says it was full. Nobody can show it. So move the check to where both sides can see it. Weigh the lot with the driver present, and photograph the reading. Read the quote back to the client on the call, line by line, before you send it. Count the stock with the store keeper and the accountant together, on a fixed date each month.
The aim is not to catch anyone. The aim is to settle the question at the moment it is cheapest to settle.
script.sees: FULL: Palak to camera. Brief cutaway to goods being weighed with a driver present.
script.title: Lesson two: a test done in front of the person removes the argument

script.say:
Third. A visible record settles the payment.
The farmer leaves with a slip. Litres, fat, rate, amount. When the money comes, she checks it against her own record.
Think of your suppliers, your contract workers, your clients. What do they hold in their hand after each transaction? Usually nothing. So they call. A simple record, shared at the moment of the work, changes that. A delivery note signed by both sides. A job card that shows the hours. A client file where the client can see what stage the work is at, and what is due from them.
When both sides hold the same record, the payment stops being a negotiation. It becomes a check.
script.sees: FULL: Palak to camera. Brief cutaway to a delivery note being signed by two hands.
script.title: Lesson three: a visible record settles the payment

script.say:
Fourth. The system grows because the rule at the smallest unit is the same everywhere.
Operation Flood did not copy Kurien. It copied the counter, more than seventy thousand times.
In a firm of forty, the smallest unit is one piece of work. One order. One quote. One client file. If each of those has a home, with a name, a date and a next step, then it does not matter whether the owner is at the desk, at a wedding, or on a plane. The rule holds.
So do not start with the whole firm. Start with one process. Make the rule at that counter the same every time. Run it for a month. Then copy it to the next process, and the next branch, without changing the rule.
That is how a small room in Samarkha became more than seventy thousand rooms across India. Not by finding seventy thousand remarkable people. By keeping one rule simple enough to repeat.
script.sees: FULL: Palak to camera. Brief cutaway to her hand writing a task with a name, a date and a next step.
script.title: Lesson four: the same rule at the smallest unit

script.say:
In my family's firm, VSP Consultants, we were the follow-up department for years. Every update, every payment question, every "is it done" came to one desk. What changed it was not working harder. It was giving the work a home, a fixed rhythm, and a record everyone could see. [your own line]
This is the work I do now, at Venture Drafters. I sit with an owner, find the one process that comes through them most often, and design its counter: the rhythm, the check and the record. We set it up on your own sheet, train your team, and manage it with you.
Four things, then. A fixed rhythm, so nobody has to chase. A check done in front of the person, so nobody has to argue. A record both sides can see, so the payment settles itself. And one rule, the same at the smallest counter, so the firm can grow without the owner in every room.
A farmer in Anand does not need to chase her payment. Your supplier should not need to either. And neither should you.
If you want to see how this looks for your business, book a 30-minute call. The link is in the description.
script.sees: FULL: Palak to camera.
script.title: What I do now

Built to Run: Stories, episode 04: Amul. Twice a day, every day, for 3.6 million people.. Source: Marketing/case-studies/04-amul.md (script, b-roll list, slide outline, fact sheet, sources, cut-downs). Fortnightly Monday slot 2026-12-21, 11:00.

Do not claim (from the fact sheet):
- That Kurien founded Amul. The farmers and Tribhuvandas Patel founded and registered the union in 1946; Kurien arrived in May 1949.
- "247 litres" as the first day's collection. The union's own pages say about 250 litres a day in June 1948. Use "about 250".
- That every society pays daily, or that Amul pays "every ten days" everywhere. The cycle varies by society and period; say "on a fixed cycle, set in advance".
- "Rs 200 crore paid daily to farmers" as evidence of a daily payment cycle. It is an aggregate value of milk bought, not a payment schedule.
- That farmers receive 80 to 85 percent of the consumer rupee, as a verified fact. It is a figure GCMMF's managing director has repeated; it is the company's own claim and has not been independently checked here.
- Rs 1 lakh crore as GCMMF's turnover. That is the wider Amul brand figure; GCMMF's own 2025-26 turnover is Rs 73,450 crore.
- That Operation Flood alone made India the world's largest milk producer. The causal link is debated.
- The story that Manthan was funded by farmers contributing two rupees each, unless separately verified.
- Any reason for Kurien's 2006 exit beyond the public record: he resigned ahead of a no-confidence motion and cited a High Court order.
- Anecdotes about Kurien's personal habits (for example, that he did not drink milk). Not verified here.
- "Within a month I left the government creamery to join the Kaira Cooperative" as the sequel to Tribhuvandas Patel's request. In the book it follows an astrologer's prediction, and the Kaira union says Kurien got his relieving order at the end of 1949.
- Rs 9,000 crore as the amount paid "over those months" of the lockdown. The source gives no period.
- A fortnightly payment cycle for farmers. No source found.
- "India's largest" or "No. 1" in Palak's own voice. Use the sourced numbers instead.

passthrough.openQuestions:
1. Payment cycle: I could verify daily, weekly and ten-day cycles (NDDB handbook; Kaira union, 2021), but not a fortnightly cycle from a source I could read. The script says "fixed and known in advance" and gives the range. If you want a current figure, one call to a Gujarat union's procurement office would settle it.
2. Which scale figure to use: April 2026 reports give about 31 million litres a day; April 2025 gives 300 lakh. The script says "about 3 crore litres a day". The 18,600 villages figure is from a 2025 news report (Medium); older GCMMF decks give 18,549 societies.
3. I Too Had a Dream: the two Kurien lines are taken from a 2024 newspaper column that quotes the book. Please check them against your copy, with page numbers, before recording.
4. Sensitivity: Kurien's 2006 exit and later board politics involve living people and political parties. The script states only the public record and names no politician. Keep it that way.
5. The cold open is a composite scene, captioned as such. If you can film at a dairy cooperative society near Indore, the opening becomes real footage; it needs written permission and no member faces or numbers on screen.
6. Web research ran out of search budget before I could confirm a current count of automatic collection units and bulk coolers across all GCMMF unions, or the Manthan funding story. Neither is used in the script.

### Fact-check log, 30 October 2026

**Confirmed**
- 4 January 1946 Samarkha meeting, 14 December 1946 registration, 15-day strike, June 1948 start, 432 farmers and 5,000 litres by end 1948 (Kaira Union history page, amuldairy.com/history.php).
- Kurien arrived 13 May 1949; roles and years (amuldairy.com/dr_kurien.php).
- "Excruciatingly unexciting and conservative" is in I Too Had a Dream (Google Books phrase search, Roli Books edition; page number not retrieved).
- Lockdown: 35 lakh litres a day, about Rs 800 crore extra (Asian Age, DeshGujarat); 10 to 15 percent more milk, Rs 42 and Rs 31 prices, 30 percent fall (Just Food).
- Rs 337 to Rs 765 per kg fat (Asian Age, DeshGujarat).
- Rs 73,450 crore, 36 lakh farmers, about 31 million litres a day (Free Press Journal, Dairy Business MEA); 18 unions, 18,600 villages (Storyboard18, FY25).
- Payment: daily, weekly or ten-day (NDDB handbook p. 61); GCMMF said weekly in November 2016 (DeshGujarat).

**Changed**
- Script said Kurien wrote "Within a month I left..." Now quotes "excruciatingly unexciting and conservative". In the book the first line follows an astrologer's prediction, so the lead-in misled.
- Script said Rs 9,000 crore was paid "over those months". Now says the managing director said Amul had put about Rs 9,000 crore into the rural economy (The Week gives no period).
- Essay and script said Rs 800 crore "worth" to producers. Now "extra to rural milk producers" (Asian Age).
- Confidence raised to High: fat price and lockdown rows.

**Still unverified**
- Fortnightly farmer payment cycle: none found in NDDB, Kaira union, GCMMF or PIB sources.
- 18,600 villages for 2026: no April 2026 report gives a count.
- Book page numbers: previews blocked.
- GCMMF's own July 2020 press release PDF: 403 error.
